Loca — The Geography of a Life

A scholarly edition of the geography of Tycho Brahe’s life: every place at which he is documented as bodily present, from birth to burial, with what he did there, whom he engaged, and the page-cited evidence for each claim, graded A–D. Holdings he never visited, an estate he declined, and legends the sources refute are recorded in the phantom register, never on the map.

62 places of documented presence · 140 stays · 21 journeys · 14 sites · 43 refuted or disputed claims · 878 page-cited references · 1546–1601, Knutstorp to the Týn church

Edition of 5 September 2026 · how to cite · data (JSON) · catalogue (CSV)

1Introduction

This is the geography of one life, assembled place by place. It records every location at which Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) is documented as bodily present, the span and purpose of each stay, the people he engaged there, and the page-cited evidence for every claim — together with the structures he built, the routes he travelled, and the places the sources show he did not visit.

It was compiled by reconciling fourteen independent sweeps of the authoritative literature — Dreyer, Thoren, Christianson, Friis, Nørlind, Gassendi, Jönsson, the Prague Crossroads volume, Studnička, Björklund, Håkansson, the royal chancery register, the meteorological diary, and the dated autograph specimens — into a single itinerary in which every disagreement between the sources is kept rather than smoothed away. Where two authorities give different dates, both are printed and the adopted reading is named.

The presence rule is absolute. A stay asserts that Tycho was physically at a place. A fief he held, a purchase he made at a distance, a book printed under his name, a summons he received, a letter addressed to him — none of these is a presence, and none appears in the itinerary or on the map. They are recorded instead in the phantom register (§9), where the circulating claim is stated and the evidence against it is given. The register is a deliverable in its own right: knowing where a man was not is part of knowing where he was.

The figures, and what they mean

FigureCountDefinition
Gazetteer records71one per location the compilation needed, including those with no documented stay
Places with a documented stay62the places at which Tycho is attested bodily present
… of which mapped55have a stay and a resolved coordinate; the map shows these and no others
Documented stays140one per attested period of presence at one place; a stay is not a visit and the count is not a count of journeys
Journeys21documented route sequences between stays
Presence claims refuted or disputed43the phantom register (§9); several are classes of claim rather than places
Sites14built structures recorded, with 25 rooms beneath them
Evidence citations878page-level citations across the register, from 38 sources

What these numbers are not. They are not a measure of how Tycho spent his life. Fifty-five years are unevenly attested: the two decades on Hven are one anchor stay, while the sixteen months of the exile carry more separate records than the first twenty-nine years together. A place with six stays is a place the sources happen to date six times, not a place he visited six times. No ratio here is a proportion of his life; no count of stays is a count of journeys made. And an absence of evidence is recorded as an absence of evidence, never as an absence of Tycho.

The evidence grades

GradeNameAs applied in this editionStaysPlacesClaims
ASecurepresence directly and multiply attested802213
BProbableattested by one strong source, or as a documented route station351824
CPossibleprobable, single-source, or regionally imprecise25265
DDoubtfulpresence claimed in a source but disputed or conjectural051

No stay is graded D: a presence that weak is not asserted as a stay at all. D survives on five gazetteer records and one refuted claim, where a source does make the assertion and the edition records that it does.

Conventions

Dates. Every span is printed at the precision its evidence supports. The stated precision belongs to the best-attested bound; where the other bound is coarser, the span names the open end rather than inventing a date — “25 May 1565 (departure within the month)”. Dates are Julian (Old Style) unless a record says otherwise, and the individual calendar notes flag the Old Style / New Style handoffs of the 1599 journey into Bohemia.

Coordinates. Where the sources agree on a location, the pin is their median and each gazetteer entry prints the spread. Well-known towns without votes carry a pin from general knowledge, marked as such. Manors and unidentified sites are left unpinned rather than guessed, and region-blob records — “Denmark (unspecified)”, “Scania (region)” — carry no pin by design.

Citations. Page references are to the printed edition; where the compilation worked from a digital copy, that copy’s page follows in parentheses (p. 22 (PDF 33)), because it is what lets the claim be re-checked against the same copy. 97 citations could be located only by the copy’s page and are left so marked rather than converted by a guessed offset; §11 counts them by source.

People. A person named on a stay who has a record in the Familia pillar is linked to it, and the link opens that record. A name without a link has no Familia record yet; §11 lists the most frequent.

Record keys. Every record prints its key (stay-rostock-1568) and is addressable: #stay-rostock-1568 as an anchor, or ?stay=stay-rostock-1568, which highlights it.

3Register of stays

The same 140 stays in full, in chronological order within the eight periods of the life. Each record carries its narrative, the people engaged, what was made or acquired there, the page-cited evidence with the sources’ own words, and — where they disagree — the disagreement.

Childhood in Scania and Zealand

1546–15595 stays

From his birth at Knutstorp on 14 December 1546 to his dispatch to the University of Copenhagen in April 1559, Tycho's childhood was shaped by his abduction, aged about one, by his childless paternal uncle Jørgen Brahe, who with his wife Inger Oxe raised the boy at his ancestral seat of Tostrup in eastern Scania and at the royal castles he successively commanded — Næsbyhoved on Funen, Vordingborg on Zealand, Nykøbing on Falster. Latin instruction began about his seventh year; whether it came from a private tutor in the uncle's house or at a grammar school (Vordingborg is only a modern presumption) is unresolved, and is the period's one genuinely soft spot.

c. 14 December 1546 – 1548

AKnutstorpstay-knutstorp-1546
family
Tycho Brahe was born at his family's ancestral seat of Knutstorp in Scania on 14 December 1546, between nine and ten in the morning by his father Otte Brahe's own memorandum; the Stephanius notes, copied from Tycho's lost self-horoscope, give 10:47 a.m. The firstborn of twins — his brother was stillborn, later the subject of his first publication (1572) — he was baptised Tyge after his paternal grandfather, Latinising the name at university. Norlind and Thoren place the birth in the medieval manor that preceded the moated brick castle Otte built from 1551. He remained with his parents Otte Brahe and Beate Bille only until about mid-1548, when, after the birth of his brother Steen (21 December 1547), his childless uncle Jørgen Brahe carried him off, 'without the knowledge of my parents', to raise as his own. Knutstorp remained his lifelong territorial designation.
Calendar. All dates Old Style (Julian); Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700. Tycho himself sometimes wrote 13 December, counting the astronomical day from noon.

The sources disagree. Birth date: Gassendi canvasses 13/14/15/19 December 1546; Norlind pp. 11–12 rejects Gassendi's 19 Dec (mis-derived Tuesday) and Jessenius' funeral-oration 15 Dec — 14 December o.s., fixed by Otte Brahe's memorandum, followed (unanimous modern). Hour: the memorandum has 'between 9 and 10'; the Stephanius horoscope notes and Gassendi have 10:47 a.m. — both recorded, not harmonised. Abduction timing: Thoren has mid-1548 (middle of the second year, after Steen was past infancy dangers); Christianson 2020, Friis and Jönsson link it to after Steen's birth at about age one; Norlind commits only to 'before his seventh year' — c. 1548 followed (Thoren/Christianson). Birth building: Norlind and Thoren argue the medieval manor, not the 1551 castle of the later tradition.

c. 1548 – April 1559

BTosterupstay-tostrup-1548
familyeducation
The fostered boyhood was based at Jørgen Brahe's ancestral seat of Tostrup in eastern Scania, where the childless Jørgen and Inger Oxe raised him as their only charge, with visits to Knutstorp to see his birth parents. From about his seventh year (c. 1553) he was put to Latin and the rudiments of learning — Dreyer and Friis with a private tutor (Hovmester) in the uncle's house, five years of schooling above all in Latin, in which he was soon writing letters and verse. Against the Brahe military tradition, Jørgen intended him for learned studies and a chancery career, and paid for his education until age eighteen. Friis, Norlind and Jönsson all hedge the Tostrup placement as inference from Jørgen's fief-holding; Thoren states it plainly. The stay, interleaved with residence at Jørgen's successive royal fiefs, closed when the boy was sent to the University of Copenhagen in April 1559.

Friis ('rimeligviis'), Norlind ('om det nu var hit han fördes') and Jönsson ('bör ha') all present Tostrup as inference from Jørgen's fief-holding rather than documented residence; Thoren asserts it most firmly (though prefacing that not even the place of upbringing is documented) — Thoren followed, hedges recorded. The schooling is a second soft spot: Dreyer and Friis have a private tutor in the uncle's house; Norlind doubts a formal cathedral Latin school altogether ('mycket ovisst'); the school is never identified in any source (see the Vordingborg stay for the 'formodentlig' school conjecture).

Jørgen Brahe was promoted from Tranekaer Castle on Langeland to the command of Næsbyhoved Castle on Funen in 1549, and Thoren judges that Inger Oxe and the infant Tyge presumably followed him on these periodic moves between fiefs, as on his frequent trips back to Tostrup and appearances at court. The boy's presence is an inference from the structure of the foster household, not a documented sighting, and no other swept source places him there; the stay is graded accordingly.

1552 – 1557 (bounds uncertain)

BVordingborgstay-vordingborg-1552

Jørgen Brahe received command of the immense medieval royal stronghold of Vordingborg on the south coast of Zealand in 1552, and Tycho passed part of his boyhood in the sprawling castle — Christianson recalls the connection when the 1597 exile caravan passed through the town. Vordingborg sat on the main route between Copenhagen and the continent: Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg came with his court in 1556, Christian III's peripatetic court stayed periodically, and Brahe, Oxe and Rud kin visited regularly — the boy's first exposure to high court traffic. The school question stays open: his autobiography has him at Latin school 'in his seventh year', and the Nationalmuseet education essay presumes ('formodentlig') Vordingborg Latin school because Jørgen was then lensmand there, but Facts of Life (1970) is silent on schooling before 1559, Dreyer and Friis have a private tutor at Tostrup instead, and Norlind doubts a formal school altogether. No school is asserted.

Queen Mother Sophie had invested Jørgen Brahe with the fief and command of Nykøbing in 1555, and in 1557, having relinquished his royal fief in the power struggle that preceded Peder Oxe's fall, Jørgen transferred his seat to the island fortress between Lolland and Falster. On Thoren's 'presumably followed' reading of the foster household, the ten-to-twelve-year-old Tycho lived there until he was sent to Copenhagen in April 1559. Christianson notes that Jørgen also commanded Nykøbing but attaches Tycho's boyhood residence only to Vordingborg; the stay is therefore single-source and inferential.

Student at Copenhagen

1559–15621 stays

Tycho's first university period: nearly three years at the University of Copenhagen, from his arrival on 19 April 1559, aged twelve, to his departure for Leipzig on 14 February 1562. Sent by his uncle and foster-father Jørgen Brahe to read rhetoric and philosophy towards a career in law and statecraft, he followed the Melanchthonian curriculum while quietly assembling his first astronomical library — Sacrobosco, the Basel 1551 Ptolemy, Apian, Regiomontanus, the ephemerides of Carelli and Stadius. The famous story that the predicted solar eclipse of 21 August 1560 awakened his vocation is Gassendi's tradition, rejected by Norlind; the book purchases are the documented fact. Danish dates are Julian throughout.

19 April 1559 – 14 February 1562

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1559
educationobservationbooks & printing
Tycho arrived at the University of Copenhagen on 19 April 1559, aged twelve — the first of his family to begin university studies — under Jørgen Brahe's plan for a career in law and statecraft, lodging in the household of a professor (unnamed in Christianson 2020; Thoren suggests possibly Niels Hemmingsen). He worked through the Melanchthonian trivium while turning himself, from 1560, into an astronomer by purchase: Sacrobosco's De sphaera (used in Scavenius's lectures), the Basel 1551 Ptolemy folio bought the last day of November 1560 for two Joachimsthaler (signed and annotated, now Prague University Library, also bearing Johannes Pratensis's name), Apian's Cosmographia and Regiomontanus's De triangulis signed 'Tycho Brahe, Anno 1561' — the first appearance of the Latinised name — and the ephemerides of Carelli (bought with Jens Nilsson) and Stadius, compared for Ptolemaic against Copernican predictions. The tradition that the predicted partial solar eclipse of 21 August 1560 awakened his vocation begins with Gassendi; Norlind rejects it as aetiological myth. He left for Leipzig on 14 February 1562.
Calendar. Danish dates Julian (Old Style) throughout.

The sources disagree. The 1560 eclipse-vocation story: Gassendi (origin), Dreyer, Christianson 2020 and Morsing assert it; Håkansson hedges ('kanske'); Norlind pp. 13–15 rejects it as aetiological myth (Tycho never mentions the eclipse, not even in his autobiography) — rendered here as tradition, not fact; the eclipse itself and the book purchases stand. Arrival 19 April 1559 rests on Stephanius' notes; Norlind warns it may be the inscription date (matricle lost 1728), and Thoren notes noblemen's sons usually only attended lectures without matriculating — day-precision kept with this caveat. Lodging: Christianson 2020 has an unnamed professor's household, Thoren offers two candidates — Scavenius (professor of mathematics, an Oxe client) and Hemmingsen — stated as possible, not merged. End date: 14 February 1562 (Dreyer, Norlind, Friis, the Nationalmuseet essays, Jönsson) adopted over Thoren's month-precision February 1562; no real conflict (Thoren's 24 March 1562 is the Leipzig registration).

Leipzig with Vedel

1562–15652 stays

The first foreign study tour: three years at Leipzig university, nominally at Germany's best law school under the governorship of Anders Sørensen Vedel, in fact the clandestine beginning of Tycho's observational astronomy. The Saturn–Jupiter conjunction of August 1563 exposed the errors of every planetary table; compasses gave way from 1 May 1564 to a transversal-divided cross-staff, his first serious instrument. The Leipzig circle — Scultetus, Homelius, Camerarius, Valentin Thau — supplied his first instrument-craft and court-astrology contacts. Framed by the outward journey via Wittenberg (February–March 1562) and the return to Denmark in May 1565.

February 1562 – March 1562

BWittenbergstay-wittenberg-1562
in transit
A waypoint of the outward journey, not yet a study station. Having crossed the southern Baltic in February 1562, Tycho and Vedel travelled up the Elbe to Wittenberg and continued overland — Thoren has them riding two more days — to Leipzig, where both were registered on 24 March 1562. Tycho's Wittenberg study residence belongs to a later period.

24 March 1562 – 17 May 1565

ALeipzigstay-leipzig-1562
educationobservationinstrumentsbooks & printing
Tycho reached Leipzig on 24 March 1562, five and a half weeks out of Copenhagen, with the twenty-year-old Anders Sørensen Vedel as preceptor, and matriculated as 'Ticho Brade ex Scandia'. Sent to read law, he lodged in a professor's household and studied astronomy secretly at night: a fist-sized celestial globe hidden from Vedel, Stadius's ephemerides, then the Alphonsine and Prutenic tables. The Saturn–Jupiter conjunction of August 1563, which the tables missed badly, prompted his first observation log, headed 'Anno 1563, seventeen years of age, Leipzig'. Sightings taken first with large compasses gave way from 1 May 1564 to a cross-staff after Gemma Frisius, transversal-divided by Bartholomaeus Scultetus, for whose faulty divisions he computed a correction table. His circle included Homelius, Camerarius and the electoral mathematician Valentin Thau; he also cast nativities, Peucer's among them. He and Vedel left on 17 May 1565.
Calendar. All dates Old Style (Julian); the period predates the 1582 Gregorian reform, so no dual dating arises.

The sources disagree. First recorded observation: Dreyer (p. 19) has 17 August 1563; Christianson 2020 (pp. 25–26) has first entry 18 August — Christianson followed (modern), Dreyer's day noted; Thoren gives only August 1563. Cross-staff origin: Thoren (pp. 18–19; his n. 27 hedges whether the two references are to one instrument) has Tycho ordering an Arscenius cross-staff from Louvain; Dreyer, Norlind and Christianson 2020 have a radius built at Leipzig after Gemma Frisius's instructions with Scultetus's transversal scale — both accounts preserved, not conflated. Norlind (p. 20) rejects Dreyer's inference of a second Leipzig sojourn in November 1565 as a copyist's misreading of the observation journal ('En andra resa till Leipzig kan det naturligtvis ej vara tal om') — no such stay created. Christianson 2000 gives no dates for Leipzig; its 1562–1565 span is this edition's approximation, not that source's assertion.

The Wanderjahre

1565–157021 stays

The Wanderjahre carry Tycho from the wartime homecoming of May 1565, through Jørgen Brahe's death, across the second and third study journeys: Wittenberg (April–September 1566, cut short by plague), Rostock (the duel of 29 December 1566 that cost him the bridge of his nose), the 1567 interlude at home, the second Rostock residence of 1568 with the Roskilde canonry promise, matriculation at Basel in autumn 1568, and the fourteen Augsburg months (April 1569 – May 1570) that produced the Quadrans Maximus at Göggingen, the first sextant and the great globe commission. The Textor album leaf (Wittenberg, 9 September 1570) and the Helsingborg observation of 30 December 1570 fix the previously obscure homeward route to his father's deathbed.

c. May 1565 – June 1565

BCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1565
in transitfamily
Landing at Copenhagen from Rostock in late May or early June 1565, Tycho learned that his foster father Jørgen Brahe — captor of the Swedish flagship in 1564 — was now vice-admiral of the fleet, deep in preparations for the next engagement. From the capital he proceeded home through Scania. Weeks later Jørgen fell into the water at the bridge between Copenhagen castle and the town while rescuing King Frederick II, and died on 21 June 1565 of the illness contracted; no source places Tycho at the deathbed or funeral, and Dreyer expressly declines to say where he resided in the following months. Norlind's pole-height list supplies independent, if inferential, support for the passage through the capital.

May 1565

BWittenbergstay-wittenberg-1565

First touch of Wittenberg, in transit on the homeward road from Leipzig in May 1565. Thoren has Tycho and Vedel pass through purposefully, to see his former instructor Bartholomew Schultz (Scultetus), who had moved there the previous autumn; Friis conjectures a call on Caspar Peucer; Gassendi records only a regretted transit (in transcursu), the regret that motivated the deliberate residence of 1566. Norlind grounds the passage independently in the pole-height list of the oldest observation journal, whose sequence Leipzig–Wittenberg–Rostock he reads as the route home, and notes that Stephanius's later phrase 'rediit Wittebergam' for 1566 presupposes this earlier visit.

Tycho and Vedel reached Rostock on 25 May 1565, eight days after leaving Leipzig (17 May, Hegelund's date) — the Baltic port's first appearance in his itinerary, as a mere embarkation point a year before it became his residence. The Northern Seven Years' War was in full course and hostile fleets cruised the Baltic, but merchant sailings continued and the pair crossed to Copenhagen without meeting hostile cruisers. The 25 May date rests on the Stephanius notes and is reported unanimously.

Travelling home through Scania in June 1565, Tycho stopped at Helsingborg — the natural landfall of the Sound crossing — and made a determination of the local latitude, the first of three such stops (Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp) that constitute his earliest recorded geodetic-astronomical fieldwork on home ground, made with the instruments and habits acquired at Leipzig. The stop rests on the pole-height list in his oldest observation journal, which Norlind reads as the itinerary of the journey itself.

c. June 1565 – April 1566

BKnutstorpstay-knutstorp-1565
familyproperty
About a year at home in Denmark between the Leipzig and Wittenberg residences, June 1565 to April 1566, bracketed by the Stephanius notes (Rostock 25 May 1565; 'returned to Wittenberg on April 15, 1566, from his fatherland'). Jørgen Brahe's death on 21 June 1565 changed Tycho's status: the plan to make him heir to Tostrup lapsed, and Inger Oxe, widowed, continued to regard him 'with a quite special love'. He recorded no observations that year, occupied himself with ordering his money matters and gathering funds for the peregrination he had resolved on, and found the nobility's contempt for his studies galling — of his relations only Steen Bille approved. By spring 1566 he had won leave, or simply asserted himself, to depart.

c. June 1565

BMalmöstay-malmo-1565
observationin transit
The second latitude-determination stop of the June 1565 homeward journey through Scania, between Helsingborg and Knutstorp. Malmö is the penultimate name in the pole-height list of the oldest observation journal (Leipzig, Wittenberg, Rostock, Copenhagen, Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp), read by Norlind as the route of the journey with observations made under way; the observations were preserved in the notebook record but not printed by Dreyer, as Thoren notes from Norlind. As with the other Scanian waypoints, the presence rests on this journal inference.

15 April 1566 – 16 September 1566

AWittenbergstay-wittenberg-1566
education
The second study journey's first station: Tycho arrived at Wittenberg on 15 April 1566, this time with the M.A. Hans Aalborg as preceptor rather than a noble hovmester, finding Vedel already there completing his degree among the traditional Danish student colony. The leading connection was Caspar Peucer, Melanchthon's son-in-law, professor of medicine and Preceptor primarius, whose teaching Tycho attended for a time — though he never formally matriculated (a lack he remedied ceremonially only in February 1599) and lodged with no professor, perhaps with Schultz. After five months plague broke out in the congested town and caused a general student exodus: he left on 16 September 1566 and reached Rostock on the 24th, an eight-day journey.

24 September 1566 – 1567

ARostockstay-rostock-1566
educationobservationalchemy & medicine
First Rostock residence: arrived 24 September 1566, matriculated in October under rector Simon Pauli, lodging in the household of the theologian Lucas Bacmeister. No one taught astronomy, but the Paracelsian Levinus Battus and the empiricist Heinrich Brucaeus opened his lifelong medical-alchemical interests. On the lunar eclipse of 28 October 1566 he posted anonymous Latin verses foretelling Sultan Süleyman's death — the sultan had died on 9 September, before the prediction. At a betrothal dance in Bacmeister's house on 10 December he quarrelled with his kinsman Manderup Parsberg; the quarrel flared again on 27 December and on 29 December, about seven in the evening in deep darkness, a duel cost Tycho the bridge of his nose, concealed thereafter by a prosthesis. He observed the solar eclipse of 9 April 1567 at Rostock — 'the first he observed as a real astronomer' — and went home in the summer of 1567, departure undated.

The sources disagree. Cause of the quarrel — the primary note is read two ways: Norlind (p. 22) renders Stephanius 'propter choream' (over the dance), while Christianson's edition of the same note (Facts of Life 1970, p. 24) has the dispute arising 'concerning the movements of the stars' at the Bacmeister betrothal; Gassendi's specific prowess-contest version rests on a misreading of Laurus and is rejected (Norlind). The underlying cause is not settled. Duel date: 10/27/29 December 1566 sequence adopted (Stephanius, Norlind, the Nationalmuseet essays); Gassendi notes some referred the incident to October 1565 — rejected. Venue: Christianson 2000 places the duel in Bacmeister's house; Thoren (Stolterfoht tradition) and Jönsson a churchyard by night — quarrel indoors, duel outside adopted. Prosthesis: Gassendi's wax-gold-silver and Dreyer's gold-and-silver composition are debunked — copper-zinc alloy (brass) with traces of gold per the 1901 and 2010 exhumations. Jessenius's funeral-oration version (an assassin's night attack) was formally protested: Christian IV's letter of 4 May 1602 insists the two duelled 'redlich fur der faust'.

c. 1567

CCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1567
educationcourt & patronagesocial visit
During the undocumented second half of 1567 Tycho 'doubtless went to the university to renew old acquaintanceships' in Copenhagen and may also have appeared at court, where Peder Oxe — his foster mother's brother — had returned from exile and was consolidating power as governor of Copenhagen and, by August 1567, lord high steward. Both the university visit and the court contact are Thoren's inferences from the changed political landscape, not documented occasions; the stay is recorded on his authority alone and graded accordingly.

c. June 1567 – December 1567

BDenmark (unspecified)stay-denmark-1567
familypropertysocial visit
Home from Rostock for the second half of 1567, scarred and wearing the prosthesis, in a country strained by the Seven Years' War: the Scanian borderlands lay wasted and his father Otte — promoted in 1567 to the front-line governorship of Helsingborg Castle — was organising a fresh offensive. Tycho ordered his affairs, visited kinsmen and friends ('better than I deserved', he later wrote of his reception), and announced against the expectations of his class that he would continue his scientific studies; Otte was among those upset, while Steen Bille, Peder Oxe, Inger Oxe and Beate Bille showed understanding. Christianson infers that the Christmas-holiday discussions with Peder Oxe and Steen Bille moved them to broker the Roskilde canonry charter that followed in spring 1568. He stayed through his twenty-first birthday and the holidays, then embarked on the third journey. No source names the residence; Thoren has him 'surely' with the family in their new Helsingborg quarters.

1568 – 1569 (bounds uncertain)

From Basel Tycho visited Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs, professor of mathematics at nearby Freiburg im Breisgau, admiring his collection of instruments and noting celestial models that demonstrated planetary motions according to the theories of Ptolemy and Copernicus — an early exposure to mechanical representations of the rival world systems, and one of the deliberate calls on astronomical authorities that punctuated this tour. The acquaintance bore fruit: in 1575 he would order a zodiacal armillary from Schreckenfuchs.

1 January 1568 (departure within the year)

ARostockstay-rostock-1568
educationobservationalchemy & medicinecourt & patronage
Second Rostock residence: Tycho dashed back without a tutor, arriving on New Year's Day 1568, lodging two weeks with the Paracelsian Levinus Battus before taking his own rooms in the Jurists' College — 'a very suitable place for observing' — and resuming observation on 2 January. His letter of 14 January 1568 to Hans Aalborg, the earliest preserved of his whole correspondence, asked him to 'bury in deep silence the cause of my departure' from home. The university levied a stiff fine of twenty Joachimsthalers, probably over the Parsberg duel; Brucaeus and Peder Oxe's influence aided the appeal, which proceeded without him. By royal letters patent dated Copenhagen 14 May 1568 — the first royal favour shown him, credited to Peder Oxe — he was promised the next vacant canonry at Roskilde cathedral, probably received at Rostock; law study yielded to his own formation, and he left, departure undated, for the south.

c. September 1568 – 1569

ABaselstay-basel-1568
educationinstruments
By September 1568 Tycho was in Basel — city of Erasmus and Paracelsus, the university Peder Oxe had known in youth and exile — where he matriculated with cousins and several other Danes under the rectorate of Simon Sulzer, probably in August or September (standing no. 52 in the year's list). After nine years of university work he had exhausted teachers and texts: here he first worked on his own, experimenting with quadrant construction assisted by the young Hugo Blotius, later imperial librarian in Vienna — probably including the gilt brass quadrant with Nonnian subdivisions and 'an emblem of life and death' later depicted in the Mechanica, though a larger design of 1–1.5 m radius proved unstable in wind. Basel lodged itself in his affections: in 1575 he would seriously consider settling there for good. He stayed through the winter, leaving for the Danube road at the end of 1568 or in early spring 1569.

c. 1569

BIngolstadtstay-ingolstadt-1569
in transitsocial visit
Passing through Ingolstadt on the Danube, Tycho called on Philip Apian — son of Peter Apian of Astronomicum Caesareum fame, whose Cosmography Tycho had used to teach himself astronomy — a keen observer of heavens and earth whose huge triangulated map of Bavaria, printed at his own officin, was one of the cartographic marvels of the age; Håkansson suggests the visit may seriously have awakened the cartographic interest Tycho later applied to the Øresund region. The visit's date is the most contested waypoint of the tour: Norlind shows Apian was expelled from Ingolstadt for suspected heresy only in October 1569, making a call in spring 1569, on the road from Basel to Augsburg, the likeliest reading — followed here with Thoren.

Timing of the Apian visit: Christianson 2020 places it on the 1568 southbound leg before Basel; Norlind argues spring 1569, en route Basel–Augsburg, from Apian's expulsion in October 1569 (against Dreyer's 1568 dating of the departure), and Thoren concurs; Gassendi, Dreyer and Håkansson place it on the 1570 homeward journey. Norlind's archival redating followed; the homeward-1570 tradition preserved here and at the homeward journey record.

c. 1569

ALauingenstay-lauingen-1569
social visitin transit
Following the Danube from Basel early in 1569 (Norlind: end of 1568 or spring 1569), Tycho called at Lauingen in Swabia on Cyprianus Leovitius, the astrologer of the Saturn-Jupiter conjunctions and ephemeride-maker whose tables he had used as a student. Invited home, he drew dinner out deep into the night in astronomical conversation — and found that this astronomer-astrologer never observed the heavens, owning no instruments and timing eclipses only with friends' clocks. The exchange sharpened his conviction that only a sustained course of observation could yield correct planetary tables, and strengthened his resolve on his chosen path. The encounter is recorded by Tycho himself (TBOO III, 221) and reported by every biographical tradition.

14 April 1569 – 16 May 1570

AAugsburgstay-augsburg-1569
instrumentsobservationalchemy & medicinesocial visiteducation
The longest stop of the tour: some fourteen months in the imperial city, his observations there running from 14 April 1569 to 16 May 1570, with departure soon after. Admiring the city's fortifications, fountains and civic culture, he settled among its humanist patriciate — the brothers Paul and Johann Baptist Hainzel, the rector-librarian Hieronymus Wolf, the schoolman Johannes Major — and here established instrument-making as his metier: his first self-designed instrument, the great half-arc, was usable by November 1569; he designed his first sextant, left as a parting gift to Paul Hainzel; and he commissioned the great celestial globe of 1.5 m, unfinished at his departure and left in Hainzel's care. With Paul Hainzel he built the gargantuan oak Quadrans Maximus at Göggingen. Wolf introduced him to Petrus Ramus, in Augsburg in April 1570, who urged an astronomy rebuilt on observation without hypotheses. He was increasingly drawn to alchemy — the 'spagyrical arts' — from this period, and left, reluctantly and somewhat impromptu, probably in May 1570.

Landlord: Christianson 2020 p. 36 names the goldsmith and Paracelsian Lorenz Thenn; Norlind pp. 25–26 a Danish countryman, magister Laurentius 'Den Danus' — plausibly the same Laurentius differently identified; both kept, neither asserted over the other. The Schissler workshop visit itself is Mosley's conjecture, not an assertion. Quadrant garden: all modern sources place it on Paul Hainzel's Göggingen estate; within Gassendi the funeral oration says Johann Baptist's garden while the index says Paul's. Departure: soon after 16 May 1570 (Thoren, Christianson 2020, Norlind) against Friis's 'toward the end of the year' — superseded by the Textor album leaf placing Tycho at Wittenberg on 9 September 1570.

The stop is Thoren's inference alone: no document places Tycho in Rostock in 1570, and the stay is recorded at the corresponding grade.

1 April 1570 – 16 May 1570

AGöggingenstay-goggingen-1570
observationinstruments
In the park of Paul Hainzel's country estate at Göggingen, just south-west of Augsburg, a crew of some twenty men erected the colossal oak Quadrans Maximus of Tycho's design — nearly 5.5 metres in radius (c. 14 cubits), brass scale divided to minutes and fractions of minutes, built in about a month, apparently March 1570, at Hainzel's cost. Tycho recorded his first observation with it on 1 April 1570 and observed at roughly weekly intervals; on 16 May 1570 he and Hainzel observed the Sun together with it for the last time. Petrus Ramus went out to the suburban villa after dinner to see 'a great machine he has invented' and debated whether an astronomy without hypotheses was possible. The quadrant — Tycho's first work with a large instrument, whose results he said agreed wholly with those later obtained in Denmark — stood in the open under tarpaulins, remained in use as late as 1577 by Norlind's account; Dreyer instead has it destroyed by storm in December 1574.

Fate of the quadrant: destroyed by storm December 1574 (Dreyer) against Norlind's 'still in use as late as 1577, and eventually decayed'.

9 September 1570

AWittenbergstay-wittenberg-1570
in transit
The one fixed point on the previously unknown homeward route from Augsburg: an album amicorum leaf of the Frenchman Claudius Textor (matriculated Wittenberg 1564), now in the Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg, carries Tycho's autograph verses — six lines on the stars inclining but not compelling the rational soul — signed 'Witteberge: Anno: 1570: sept: 9.' It is the oldest known Tycho album autograph, and Norlind's discovery of it proved Tycho was in Wittenberg on 9 September 1570, certainly on the journey home to Denmark, nearly four months after his last Augsburg observation. The unhurried pace tells against the tradition that his father's illness triggered the departure.

30 December 1570 – 9 May 1571

AHelsingborgstay-helsingborg-1570
familyobservation
The Wanderjahre's terminus: summoned home with his brothers as their father's health failed, Tycho was at Helsingborg Castle — Otte Brahe's seat as governor — by the end of 1570; Thoren has him home probably by the time the Stettin peace was concluded (13 December, the eve of his 24th birthday). The first documented trace is an observation of 30 December 1570 from the castle (Venus and Jupiter per Dreyer; the journals cited at X, 37), made with one of the cross-staffs that were the only instruments he still possessed — the same season the treaty ending the war was signed. Otte, who had called his sons home and compiled a legal listing of his estate, was bedridden by spring and died on 9 May 1571 after a severe three-day ague, aged 53, his family around the bed; Tycho poured out his grief in the letter to Vedel of 18 May 1571. Knutstorp passed jointly to Tycho and Steen; burial was at Kågeröd church.
Calendar. Start anchored to the first documented observation (30 December 1570); arrival by mid-December possible per Thoren/Christianson 2020.

Herrevad, the nova, the lectures, the grand tour

1570–157624 stays

Otte Brahe's death at Helsingborg in May 1571 made Tycho a Scanian landowner; he divided the early 1570s between Knutstorp, his uncle Steen Bille's proto-industrial Herrevad Abbey, and Copenhagen. At Herrevad on 11 November 1572 he saw the new star in Cassiopeia, published as De nova stella (1573) — his first book, though not his first publication. He formed his lifelong union with Kirsten Jørgensdatter, lectured at the University of Copenhagen from 23 September 1574, and in 1575 made the grand tour — Kassel, Frankfurt, Basel, Venice, Augsburg, Regensburg (Rudolf II's coronation, 1 November), Saalfeld, Wittenberg — privately resolving to emigrate to Basel before reporting to Frederick II at Sorø at Yuletide.

1571 – 1575 (bounds uncertain)

AHerrevad Abbeystay-herrevad-1571
alchemy & medicineobservationinstrumentsfamily
From late 1571 Tycho lived mainly with his maternal uncle Steen Bille, who held the secularised Cistercian abbey of Herrevad and ran it as a proto-industrial seat: glassworks with Italian blowers, the first paper mill in Skåne (which Tycho helped build), the Eket ironworks, smiths and cabinetmakers. Bille fitted out a chemical laboratory for him outside the abbey wall, and chemistry absorbed him wholly — not a single astronomical observation survives between 30 December 1570 and November 1572. On the evening of 11 November 1572, walking from the laboratory to supper, he saw the brilliant new star in Cassiopeia near the zenith, confirmed it by servants and passing peasants, and measured its distances through the winter with the newly finished walnut sextant built by the abbey's craftsmen, proving it beyond parallax — the observations published in De nova stella (1573) that redirected his life.

1571 – 1575 (bounds uncertain)

AKnutstorpstay-knutstorp-1571
propertyfamilyobservation
The family seat anchored Tycho's Scanian years: he and his brother Steen co-inherited Knutstorp at Otte Brahe's death, both styling themselves 'of Knudstrup' for life, while their mother Beate Bille kept dower occupancy. Here she revealed his stillborn twin, prompting the Latin elegy printed in 1572 as his first publication; here he formed his union with Kirsten Jørgensdatter, their first daughter born in October 1573. The De nova stella preface is dated 'Knusdorp', 5 May 1573; an ague kept him home that summer. On 8 December 1573 he observed the lunar eclipse foretold in his book with the new gilt-brass quadrant, assisted by his sister Sophie — his own note records 'Hanc ego Eclipsin in curia mea Knusdorpiana observavi diligenter'. Settlement of the paternal estate ran to spring 1575, from which he drew about 650 dalers a year.

May 1571 – 1575 (bounds uncertain)

CHelsingborgstay-helsingborg-1571

Tycho owned town houses in Helsingborg, below the castle his father had commanded until 1571, and Kirsten Jørgensdatter probably lived in one of them — 'formodligen periodvis ensam' in Håkansson's phrase — while Tycho spent ever more time at Herrevad. Christianson suggests it was perhaps in Helsingborg that he gave her the keys to larder, cabinets and doors, the act which under Danish common law made an openly cohabiting commoner a binding morganatic wife after three winters. The daughters Kirstine (b. 1573) and Magdalene (b. 1574) were raised there; little Kirstine died of plague in the town on 24 September 1576 and was buried in the Maria church, where Tycho's Latin epitaph for her survives. Tycho's own stays in the house are implied by the household, not documented.

1572

CCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1572b
books & printing
In 1572, per Christianson, Tycho took his Latin ode to his stillborn twin to the printer Mads Vingaard in Copenhagen and had it printed as his first publication — the broadsheet Carmen that antedates De nova stella by a year. The visit ties him bodily to the capital's printing trade at the very start of his publishing career, a decade before his own press on Hven. The printing itself is bibliographically certain (Nielsen 424); Tycho's personal presence at the press rests on Christianson's formulation alone.

c. 1572 – 1573

CKågerödstay-kagerod-1572

Knutstorp's parish church stood in Kågeröd, where Pastor Jørgen Hansen's daughter Kirsten Jørgensdatter lived — 'of whom little is known except that Tycho was drawn to her'. The liaison that became his lifelong common-law marriage began here in the early 1570s; around February 1573 Kirsten became pregnant with his first child, and Pratensis teased him in a letter invoking Venus, 'perhaps thinking of Tycho and Kirsten from Kågeröd'. Christianson elsewhere suggests he first saw her 'perhaps in Kågeröd church'. His bodily presence in the village is implied by the courtship rather than recorded as a dated visit.

20 July 1572 – 21 July 1572

CCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1572a
court & patronagesocial visit
For King Frederick II's marriage to Sophie of Mecklenburg, held 20 July 1572 in Copenhagen Castle, the whole Danish nobility was summoned in new court attire; the next day the young queen rode to her coronation at Our Lady's, Peder Oxe carrying her crown, amid banquets, tourneys and university festivities. Thoren states Tycho 'probably borrowed attendants for the occasion and went too'; Christianson has him enrolled as a noble courtier during the wedding week, which implies presence. A probable rather than sighted attendance, at the festivity that bound him formally to the court whose patronage would shortly transform his life.

c. 1573

BCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1573a
social visitbooks & printing
Early in 1573 Tycho came to Copenhagen with the manuscript of his Diarium and account of the new star, lodging as was his custom with Johannes Pratensis, professor of medicine. Pratensis had not yet heard of the star; the French envoy Charles de Dançay, dining them, thought Tycho was mocking Danish savants until a clear evening let him point the star out in the sky. Pratensis urged printing; Tycho demurred — partly the little work's want of polish, mainly the prejudice that authorship ill became a nobleman — and returned to Scania with his manuscript. The visit sat within a periodic Copenhagen pattern of these years, his circle led by Pratensis and the long-serving envoy Dançay, more than thirty years his senior. To the same pattern belongs Pratensis's surviving invitation to his Martinmas feast of 11 November 1573 — coincidentally the first anniversary of the nova discovery — though Tycho's attendance is nowhere documented.

c. 1573

BCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1573b
books & printingsocial visitinstruments
During a second visit in spring 1573, after German pamphlets full of nonsense about the star had reached him, Tycho was pressed to publish not only by Pratensis but by his kinsman Peter Oxe, high treasurer of Denmark, who even suggested hiding his name in an anagram. He yielded — his consent must have preceded 16 April 1573, when Pratensis reported the figures being cut — and De nova stella was elegantly printed by Lorentz Benedicht, appearing early in the summer with the star still visible; the publication details kept him occupied past the normal spring departure times and postponed his planned journey abroad by a year. To the same Copenhagen orbit of 1573 belong the commissions to the royal clockmaker Steffen Brenner for the gilt-brass quadrant and a clockwork celestial globe.

March 1574 – May 1574

AHerrevad Abbeystay-herrevad-1574
observation
A documented observing run at Herrevad in the spring of 1574, part of the Skåne-Øresund circuit recorded in Tycho's own observation books: chiefly distance-measures of planets from fixed stars with the sextant, 'satis exquisite, subtracta instrumenti parallaxi', a small quadrant also mentioned. The 1746 compiler of Danske Magazin, reading the manuscript observation books, names March and April; Dreyer, from the same books, extends the run into May, after which Tycho removed to Copenhagen for the rest of the year.

24 April 1574 – March 1575 (bounds uncertain)

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1574
educationcourt & patronagefamilyobservation
Tycho observed at Copenhagen on 24 April 1574 and spent most of the rest of the year in the city, where his daughter Magdalene was born (day and month unrecorded) and where he kept a large town house, probably with Kirsten. Urged by Pratensis and Dançay and decided by King Frederik's own request, he opened his university lectures on 23 September 1574 with the oration on the mathematical sciences — delivered before Dançay and virtually the whole university community, defending a reformed astrology and reaching public accommodation with Niels Hemmingsen — then lectured four mornings a week on planetary theory, treating Copernicus's models in geostatic form: among the first university lectures on Copernican astronomy anywhere, and he the only nobleman of his era to teach at Copenhagen. The student Peter Jacobsen Flemløs entered his service. The lectures closed around the turn of 1574–75; before departing he wrote the Latin rag-poem asking Danish women for linen so Vedel's Saxo could be printed on Scanian paper, and left as a grand seigneur about March 1575.
Calendar. Danish dates Julian (Old Style), per the Stephanius notes.

On 20 December 1574 Tycho and his brothers Steen and Axel presented themselves to King Frederick II at Sorø Abbey and took their leave of the court — the brothers to marry in 1575, Tycho to abandon the Copenhagen classroom and travel abroad, carrying a royal commission to scout artists, artisans and technicians for the Kronborg project. c. 1575

ABaselstay-basel-1575
in transiteducationother
Continuing southwest from Frankfurt, Tycho stayed some time at Basel and found it so agreeable that he resolved to settle there or nearby with his family: pure clear air and cheap living, an academy full of distinguished men in the Erasmian tradition, and above all the city's position at the meeting-point of Germany, France and Italy, whence his findings could spread and correspondence flow. Gassendi's funeral-oration source confirms that, returning homeward, he had fixed on 'Basileam Rauracorum, aut vicinum aliquem locum' as the chosen seat of his life. He deferred the final decision but carried the secret plan home at year's end — the private agenda that shaped the whole sequel, since Frederick II's offer of Hven in February 1576 was designed to forestall exactly this emigration.

c. 1575

On the return from Venice Tycho crossed the Brenner Pass before the fall snows made it uncertain and 'slipped through to Innsbruck', travelling a few days north to Augsburg — a pure transit waypoint in Thoren's account. Norlind holds the much-travelled Brenner road (Innsbruck, Trento, Treviso — the road Montaigne took five years later) to be the probable route of the outward journey as well, and the homeward journey probably retraced it. c. 1575

AVenicestay-venice-1575
social visitin transitcourt & patronage
Crossing the Alps from Basel, Tycho reached Venice — the farthest south he ever travelled — and stayed from some days to a few weeks. His own testimony survives (Progymnasmata; TBOO III, 234): about sixteen years on he recalled hearing very many Venetians, including men of the highest nobility, disputing acutely on lofty philosophical matters — words Norlind reads as attendance at the patrician learned academies, held in palaces such as the Morosini. He admired the 'splendid and grand' city, 'the Emporium of all Europe', and its most prudent government; saw the new Renaissance architecture of the Veneto, above all Palladio's, which fed directly into the Uraniborg villa ideal; and as Frederick II's agent made contacts among Venetian artisans for the Elsinore works. More than twenty years later he sent the Republic and Doge Grimani each a Mechanica with the manuscript star catalogue.

March 1575 – April 1575

AKasselstay-kassel-1575
observationinstrumentscourt & patronagesocial visit
First station of the 1575 tour: Tycho arrived with Flemløs a few days before Easter (3 April 1575) at the court of Landgrave Wilhelm IV, who had observed from the Zwehrer Thor since 1561. For more than a week — Gassendi says eight or ten days — the two conversed by day and observed by night: the nova's parallax, the retardation of the sun at the horizon (the refraction problem Tycho resolved to pursue, recalling Bernhard Walther), the position of Spica, the landgrave's azimuth quadrants, great celestial clock and Baldewein globe. Gifts were exchanged — the landgrave's star catalogue for De nova stella. When the infant Sidonia, taken ill on Maundy Thursday, died the day after Easter, Tycho withdrew as the court went into mourning. They never met again; the landgrave's later embassy to Frederik II urged support for Tycho. Tycho's own fond memories of the stay are printed (TBOO VI, 10 and 34).

April 1575

AFrankfurt am Mainstay-frankfurt-1575
books & printingin transit
Leaving mourning Kassel in April 1575, Tycho went to Frankfurt am Main for the spring book fair. He stayed some days, turning over a great variety of books and buying not a few — above all whatever published tracts on the new star of 1572 he did not yet possess, the pamphlets he would later dissect in the Progymnasmata. Thoren reconstructs the breadth of the purchases: Proclus, pseudo-Ptolemaic astrologica, Synesius, Bonatti, recent Philippist authors, French and Italian treatises including du Chesne and five works of Oronce Fine, Gesner's bibliography, and works on mining and minerals serving the alchemical interests. The stop ties the tour to his lifelong book-buying practice — in 1579 he would send Vedel to this fair with a marked-up catalogue.

c. August 1575 – October 1575

AAugsburgstay-augsburg-1575
instrumentssocial visitin transit
In late summer 1575 Tycho and Flemløs came from Italy to Augsburg, renewing the old circle — the Hainzel brothers, Hieronymus Wolf — though the second stay proved anticlimactic: the great Göggingen quadrant had been destroyed by a windstorm in December 1574 and left unrepaired, and Schissler's long-awaited celestial globe, ordered in 1570, proved imperfectly spherical and cracked at the joints. He prepared the globe for transport — it was freighted with great difficulty to Denmark the following year, trued with parchment, clad in brass and perfected on Hven, carrying the stars of his catalogue by 1595. He recruited the portrait artist Tobias Gemperlin into his service, the future painter of the mural-quadrant portrait, and scouted artisans for Frederick II, lingering into late October before dropping downriver to the Regensburg coronation.

c. October 1575 – November 1575

ARegensburgstay-regensburg-1575
court & patronagesocial visitbooks & printing
Tycho attended the Regensburg festivities for the coronation of Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans, performed with great solemnity on 1 November 1575 — his first bodily crossing of the path of the prince who would become his last patron. He had hoped to find Landgrave Wilhelm, who alone among the German princes did not come; instead he met the imperial physician Thaddaeus Hagecius, and in a few days the two formed a lifelong bond: Hagecius gave him his Dialexis on the new star, Munosius's Spanish tract, and — a most precious gift — a manuscript of Copernicus's unprinted Commentariolus, which Tycho later circulated to German astronomers, reciprocating with du Chesne's new book from Frankfurt. Hugo Blotius and Gemperlin were in the company; a manuscript De directionum significationibus he examined with Hagecius here was still on his mind in 1585 (TBOO VI, 95). Soon after the coronation he started for home to prepare the intended spring emigration.

November 1575

BNurembergstay-nuremberg-1575
social visitinstrumentsin transit
Starting north after the coronation, Tycho stopped in Nuremberg, centre of the German clock and instrument trade. He met Joachim Camerarius the Younger, physician-son of the humanist — the friendship 'contracted in a short time' that Tycho's first letter to him of November 1576 (TBOO VII, 42) fixes to this visit — and visited the shop of the fountain-maker Georg Labenwolf, whom he recommended for the Kronborg works and who later built Uraniborg's hydraulics. The contacts made here brought Nuremberg artisans to Denmark in 1577; the sculptor Johan Gregor van der Schardt was probably first met here or at Regensburg.

c. November 1575

BSaalfeldstay-saalfeld-1575
social visitbooks & printingin transit
On the road home Tycho visited Erasmus Reinhold the Younger at Saalfeld in Thuringia — the physician-son of the calculator of the Prutenic Tables, himself author of a tract on the new star. Reinhold showed him his father's surviving manuscripts, notably the Tables enriched with planetary equations of centre (prosthaphaereses) painstakingly tabulated for every ten minutes of anomaly, and — per Christianson — the elder Reinhold's annotations in Copernicus's De revolutionibus; he also gave Tycho the Almanach Astrologicum he had compiled for the previous year, for the sake of its matter on the new star. A formative encounter with the working papers behind the tables Tycho had just been lecturing from.

c. November 1575 – December 1575

BWittenbergstay-wittenberg-1575
in transitinstrumentssocial visit
The last recorded station of the tour. At Wittenberg Tycho sought out Wolfgang Schuler, who had observed the new star with a parallax of nineteen minutes, expressly to inspect the instruments behind the figure: the large wooden triquetrum (probably built by Johannes Praetorius), still locally regarded as a great achievement, which Tycho found by no means as excellent as reported — marvelling that respected astronomers could think such a mean instrument sufficient — and the wooden quadrant with which the elder Reinhold had fixed the Wittenberg pole altitude, whose value Tycho judged nearly a sixth of a degree too great. He also found the university in chaos from the Elector's crypto-Calvinist purge, Caspar Peucer imprisoned, before completing the journey home to Denmark by the year's end.

c. December 1575 – February 1576

AKnutstorpstay-knutstorp-1575
propertyfamily
Home about the end of 1575, Tycho made Knutstorp his base for the winter, secretly resolved to sell his share of the estate, buy property at Basel and leave Denmark for good — lying awake, in Christianson's phrase, wondering how he could escape. The Sorø, Copenhagen and Herrevad consultations of the following weeks all radiated from this base. In the early dawn of 11 February 1576, before he had risen from bed, a royal page who had ridden through the night was brought to his bedside with Frederik II's command to attend him in Zealand at once. The summons and its sequel belong to the next period.

December 1575

ASorø Abbeystay-soro-abbey-1575
court & patronage
Back from the continental tour toward the end of 1575, Tycho presented himself to Frederick II at Sorø Abbey, where the court had come for the Yuletide. He reported his recruiting mission — glassmakers, papermakers, painters, sculptors and hydraulic engineers from Hesse-Kassel, Augsburg, Nuremberg and Venice, recommending Gemperle, Schardt and Labenwolf for the Kronborg project — and told of the courts he had visited and the Regensburg coronation, supping with the king at Abbot Iver Bertelsen's table. The king, primed by the returning Danish embassy carrying Landgrave Wilhelm's strong recommendation, received him with exceptional graciousness and asked him to name his requirements in fiefs and honours — Hammershus, Visborg, Helsingborg and Landskrona were the class of option. Tycho, privately set on Basel, demurred and was told to think it over; he afterwards wrote frankly to Pratensis refusing the 'golden shackles' of castle-holding.

The lord of Hven

1576–159650 stays

Between the pre-dawn royal summons of 11 February 1576 and the coronation autumn of 1596, Tycho held the island of Hven as a lifetime fief and built there Uraniborg, Stjerneborg, the laboratory, printing office and paper mill. The grant sequence ran Ibstrup (11 February), Frederiksborg (18 February), first landing on Hven (22 February), the formal enfeoffment (23 May) and the foundation stone (8 August 1576). The continuous residence is one anchor stay; around it cluster the documented off-island trips — Copenhagen herredage, lawsuits and marriage negotiations, homage at Lund, weddings at Ribe and Bygholm, comet work at Helsingborg — until Christian IV's coronation opened the withdrawal of favour.

1576 – 1597 (bounds uncertain)

BCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1576b
propertysocial visitbooks & printing
Throughout the Hven years Tycho went frequently to Copenhagen, as the Meteorological Diary shows, though nothing is known of his domestic arrangements there and no observations were made in the city. He owned a house in Farvergade in the south-west of the town; on 13 March 1589 the young king's government ordered the burgomasters to lend him the adjoining stone tower on the rampart for astronomical use (revocable if needed for defence), and on 25 March 1589 he received two empty houses next his own on condition of housing the displaced dyer. Dreyer counts the very frequent trips to Copenhagen and Scania among the burdens of the island residence, especially in winter. This recurring record anchors the diary-attested habit; individually documented Copenhagen trips stand as their own stays.

1576 – 29 March 1597 (bounds uncertain)

AVen (Hven)stay-hven-1576b
observationinstrumentsbooks & printingalchemy & medicinecourt & patronagepropertyfamily
The two-decade anchor residence. Frederik II's forleningsbrev of 23 May 1576 granted Hven rent-free for life so long as he pursued his mathematical studies, with 400 daler toward a house; Dançay laid Uraniborg's foundation stone at sunrise on 8 August 1576, and the solar series begun on Tycho's thirtieth birthday, 14 December 1576, opened an unbroken observational run to 15 March 1597. He commuted from the mainland until autumn 1576; Kirsten and the children settled from late 1577, the household moving into Uraniborg in November 1580. Around it grew Stjerneborg (from 1584), the sixteen-furnace laboratory, the instrument workshop, the printing office (1584) and paper mill (1592), and a familia of up to a dozen assistants; De mundi (1588) and the Epistolae astronomicae (1596) issued from the island press, and the comet of 13 November 1577 was sighted from his fishponds. Royal visitors included Queen Sophie (1586), James VI of Scotland (20 March 1590) and the king-elect Christian (3 July 1592, the gilt globe exchanged for the king's portrait on a gold chain). Dated Uraniborg autographs pin bodily presence across 1586–1596. Every documented off-island trip is itemised as its own stay.
Calendar. Danish dates Julian throughout (Denmark kept the Julian calendar to 1700); the fief grant is dated 23 May 1576 (Kancelliets Brevboger).

The sources disagree. Foundation-stone date: Tycho's Mechanica gives 8 August 1576, the Lund fragment reads 1 August; Norlind supports 8 August astronomically (moon in Aquarius) — 8 August adopted. Departure date: 29 March 1597 (Thoren from Tycho's own statement; Dreyer's conclusion against the ledger's impossible '29 Aprilis'; Jönsson 'probably') vs 11 April (Christianson, diary entry of the household entering the Copenhagen museum) vs 29 April (Nielsen) — 29 March adopted for the end of residence, final resolution left to the period-7 reconciliation. Gassendi's index dates Christian's royal visit 1591; all modern sources 3 July 1592 — 1592 followed. Norlind (after Yrwing 1955) reads the departure as a feint to force restoration of income, which Thoren registers and finds unconvincing. Bjorklund's Bilag 4 dates the prebend loss 1596; Christianson/Thoren document the Roskilde canonry's transfer to Friis on 10 June 1597. First Hven solar observation: 14 December 1576 (Dreyer, Thoren, Jönsson) vs 13 December (Christianson 2020 p. 85) — 14 December adopted.

1576 – 1597 (bounds uncertain)

BScania (region)stay-scania-1576
propertyfamilyin transit
Dreyer attests very frequent trips from Hven across the Sound to Scania throughout the residence years — Tycho held Knutstorp jointly until its sale (before 10 August 1594), the eleven Helsingborg-county farms and the Kullagaard fief, and kept an elk on his Scanian estate — but names specific destinations only rarely (Lund 1584, the Kullen order). Recorded at region level as the source states it; the individually documented Scanian stays (Helsingborg, Lund, Knutstorp, Eriksholm, Landskrona) stand separately.

c. 1576

CTågalyckastay-tagalycka-1576
familyin transit
In the plague autumn of 1576 Tycho lodged Kirsten and Magdalene with the widow Margrethe Gagge at Tagalycka manor — his own presence inferred only from the act of escorting them. Kirsten gave birth there to a son on 2 January 1577 who died after six days; Tycho never saw the infant, and so was demonstrably absent at that point, composing a dolorous epitaph for his grave. Margrethe Gagge died 7 October 1577, whereupon Kirsten and Magdalene moved to Hven.

Presence is C-grade inference; the explicit absence at the January 1577 birth is recorded in the phantom register.

February 1576

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1576
social visitcourt & patronage
From Herrevad Tycho went on to Copenhagen and talked the king's offer over with his best friend Johannes Pratensis and the French envoy Charles de Dançay — the two learned friends who had long urged him toward astronomy and who would donate the Uraniborg cornerstone. He privately told Dancey, himself an emigre after decades as ambassador, of the plan to leave Denmark, and inquired into Pratensis's failing health; Pratensis divined his inclinations and wrote at the end of January assuring him his interests were respected in Denmark. Only after this consultation, and further discussion with Kirsten, his mother and his brother Steen, did he decide to accept.

February 1576

AHerrevad Abbeystay-herrevad-1576
social visitcourt & patronage
In the days after the Ibstrup audience Tycho rode to Herrevad Abbey to discuss the king's proposal with his uncle Steen Bille, who had himself acted as a broker of patronage in shaping it. The consultation weighed the abandoned alternative squarely: with Peder Oxe dead since October 1575, selling his half of Knutstorp to fund a Basel establishment would entangle his mother and brother, and refusing the king's generosity would reflect on all his relations. Herrevad was the first stop of a deliberate circuit — Herrevad, then Copenhagen — before Tycho resolved to accept Hven.

The sources disagree. Christianson followed (archival, Tycho's own account); Thoren's earlier dating preserved here.

10 February 1576 – 16 February 1576

AKnutstorpstay-knutstorp-1576
familycourt & patronage
Tycho lay awake at Knutstorp planning how to slip away to Basel without alerting his relatives when, about two hours before dawn on 11 February 1576, a royal courier who had ridden all night arrived commanding him to the king at Ibstrup. He returned to Knutstorp the next day, 12 February, to contemplate the offer of Hven, struck that the courier had come at the very moment of his escape plan. From here he wrote the long letter to Pratensis describing the audience, consulted his mother, brother Steen and Kirsten, then rode out to Herrevad and Copenhagen before accepting at Frederiksborg on the 18th.

11 February 1576

AIbstrupstay-ibstrup-1576
court & patronage
Obeying the pre-dawn summons, Tycho rode from Knutstorp the same day and reached the royal hunting lodge of Ibstrup (later Jaegersborg) north of Copenhagen before sunset. The chamberlain Niels Parsberg — brother of his Rostock duelling opponent — showed him into the royal chamber, where in a long private audience Frederick II, who knew of the Basel emigration plan and had lately viewed Hven from the rising Kronborg, offered him the island for his experiments in astronomy and distillation, promising buildings and income so that foreigners would come to Denmark to see and learn. Tycho noted the island's dangerous landings, promised serious consideration, and was told to bring his answer to Frederiksborg. His own account, written three days later, is the primary source.

18 February 1576

AFrederiksborgstay-frederiksborg-1576
court & patronage
One week after the Ibstrup audience, having consulted Pratensis and Dançay and certainly his mother, brother and Steen Bille, Tycho rode on 18 February 1576 to Frederiksborg Castle and accepted his sovereign's offer, renewing his service to Frederick II on new terms: an immediate annual pension of 500 dalers — nearly doubling his income — against his promise to be loyal and ready to serve when summoned. This audience formalised the contract of service that framed the whole Hven enterprise; the formal grant of the island followed on 23 May 1576, quit and free, with 400 dalers toward a residence.

22 February 1576

AVen (Hven)stay-hven-1576
observationpropertyin transit
Four days after the Frederiksborg audience Tycho crossed to the island in the Øresund to acquaint himself with his new workplace — his first known visit, as its incoming lord over Tuna's freeholding peasants — and the same evening took his first observation there, a close conjunction of Mars and the moon ('Observatio haec facta in Huenna'). The formal fee of the island followed by royal letter given at Frederiksborg on 23 May 1576, the same day the treasurer Walkendorff was ordered to pay 400 daler toward building a house on Hven — the first documentary trace of Uraniborg.

c. May 1576 – September 1576

BHelsingborgstay-helsingborg-1576
familydeath & burialin transit
Until September 1576 Tycho probably commuted to Hven from Helsingborg, where Kirsten and the children were living. That month an epidemic sweeping from Copenhagen into Skåne carried off his eldest daughter Kirstine, not quite three; Tycho buried her in the church at Helsingborg and commissioned the bronze plaque, still in the church wall, recording her as his filiola naturalis who lived two years, eleven months, eleven days and eleven hours. For safety he took little Magdalene and the pregnant Kirsten out of the town and lodged them with the noble widow Margrethe Gagge at Tagalycka manor.

c. September 1576 – December 1576

CLandskronastay-landskrona-1576
in transit
After the September 1576 epidemic broke up the Helsingborg arrangement, Tycho probably went south to Landskrona and commuted across to Hven from there, unless he already had island quarters that would take him but not the family; by the end of the year he clearly had such quarters, observing on Hven through the Christmas holidays. The Landskrona lodging is Thoren's stated probability, not a documented residence, and is graded accordingly.

A Latin letter written from Knudstrup on 3 September 1576 to the royal physician Peder Sorensen (Severinus) offers to pay for a monument to the recently dead Johannes Pratensis if Sorensen will compose the inscription; the monument was erected in Frue Kirke, Copenhagen. Document-grade evidence that Tycho was at his half-inherited family seat weeks after Uraniborg's foundation stone was laid — the dateline pair with the 21 November letter from 'Our Island of Hven' fixes the shift of his base onto the island during the first building season's autumn.

1 July 1577

BHelsingør / Kronborgstay-kronborg-1577
court & patronage
On 1 July 1577 Tycho delivered at Kronborg the extensive horoscope for the crown prince Christian, born 12 April 1577 — written in Latin with a summarising German section for Queen Sophie. It predicted a problem-free childhood, survival of a grave illness at about twelve, a life of 56-57 years under God's reservation, and a character fond of hunting and war; Tycho stressed that a four-minute error of the castle clock at the birth could overturn the whole prognosis. The astrologer-royal-adviser role in full function, five kilometres across the Sound from his building site.

c. 1578

CHelsingør / Kronborgstay-kronborg-1578
court & patronagesocial visit
On a visit to Kronborg around 1578 Tycho met the master mason Hans van Steenwinckel, experienced in architectural design with a knack for perspective drawing; he invited him to Hven, taught him geometry, astronomy and Vitruvian architectural theory, and made him the practical builder of Uraniborg's complex roofs and later designer of Stjerneborg and the Hven mill house. Kronborg was the court pole of Tycho's world — artisans like Schardt and Labenwolf worked at both castle and villa — and such visits doubtless recurred, though this is the only one Christianson individually attests.

20 October 1580 – 27 October 1580

AHelsingborgstay-helsingborg-1580

During the comet of October 1580 Tycho notes in his own observation record that he observed it at Helsingborg from 20 to 27 October, while on Hven it was observed by 'Petrus and Paulus' — Peder Jakobsen Flemløs and the visiting Wroclaw mathematician Paul Wittich, working with a quadrant while Tycho used a radius across the Sound. A week's documented absence from the island, and a rare instance of Tycho conducting coordinated parallel observations from the mainland during the Hven decades; the town lay in the len whose Kulla farms he then held.

He had sent his new Equatorial Armillary back for adjustments on 20 August before departing. The connection made here mattered: Lange's visit to Uraniborg followed a month later with his 'boy' Nicolaus Reymers in tow, seeding both the Ursus plagiarism feud and, through Sophie Brahe's later betrothal to Lange, the Urania Titani poem.

18 August 1588 – 23 August 1588

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1588

Four months after Frederick II's death, Tycho sailed to Copenhagen on Sunday 18 August 1588 and stayed several days, speaking with the regents and mobilising his allies to secure Uraniborg's future under the new government. The lobbying — begun with visits by Kaas, Rosenkrantz and Vedel to Hven in July — bore fruit at once: on 23 August 1588 the Regency Council issued a patent proclaiming its desire to perpetuate the work of the Hven observatory, the crown having already agreed on 12 July to pay 6,000 dalers toward his building debt.

Plague on Hven had forced postponement of the king-elect's intended visit (Tycho sent his pupil Cort Axelsen across on 30 April 1592 to warn him off at the shore). Christian came to Hven on 3 July with three councillors, exchanged gifts — the self-moving gilt brass globe against a gold chain with his portrait — and promised support for training young men in navigation and astronomy. 6 November 1594 – 18 November 1594

Tycho was in Copenhagen for almost two weeks, 6–18 November 1594, negotiating the terms and date of Magdalene's wedding to Gellius Sascerides. After continued negotiation through Gellius's spokesman Mogens Dallin, 15 December 1594 was fixed for the betrothal-or-wedding (the parties themselves seemed confused between the two); Gellius called on Tycho the next day, thanked him, and promised to act toward him as a son should. Tycho returned to Hven on 18 November believing the negotiations concluded.

30 November 1594 – 4 December 1594

When Gellius raised new demands, Tycho sailed back into Copenhagen on 30 November 1594, presumably to attend to the wedding details, and conferred with his sister Sophie Brahe. On the evening of Tuesday 3 December he sent Niels Krag and Mogens Dallin to Gellius, who gave no clear answer; enraged, Tycho had a full summary of events drawn up and signed by Dallin, Krag, Else Mule, Sophie and himself. Next morning he stopped at Niels Krag's home to collect two Latin wedding verses of his own composing, stayed to dinner, declared he would leave public accusation to the Good Lord, and after dinner returned with Sophie to Hven — the diary noting on 4 December 'Rediit T. B. cum sorore S. B.' — to break the sad news to Magdalene. His formal declaration cancelling the wedding contract followed on 12 December.

to 21 January 1595 (arrival within the month)

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1595
familycourt & patronage
In January 1595 Tycho was back in Copenhagen, where he first heard of the exchange between his friends and Gellius at Venusin's house a month earlier — gossip he judged to stem from Gellius's bragging around the city — and resolved to set the record straight. Rather than trying his complaint in Consistory, the university authorities mediated a settlement: a new contract dated Copenhagen 16 January 1595, signed by Rector Nicolaus Theophilus, Bishop Peter Winstrup and professors Anders Krag, Niels Krag and Anders Christensen, by which Gellius promised not to disturb Tycho or his family. Before leaving town Tycho had Anders Krag write up his account of the December scene; he returned to Hven on 21 January to bring the news to Magdalene and her mother.

10 January 1596 – 20 January 1596

ALundstay-lund-1596

To clear his name where Gellius now resided, Tycho travelled to Lund in January 1596 accompanied by Peter Frandsen, spoke with officials of the cathedral chapter, and put five written questions to Gellius at hearings before the chapter on 10 and 20 January 1596; Gellius promised answers within six weeks. The meteorological journal's note that Tycho was 'gone to Helsingborg and Skåne for ten days in January' evidently covers this circuit via Helsingborg. Immediately after the second hearing he wrote to Jørgen and Holger Rosenkrantz to shield the proceedings from court interference; on 5 February a royal missive ordered the Lund chapter to sit as a marriage court in the case.

21 February 1596 – March 1596

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1596
familycourt & patronageother
On 21 February 1596 Tycho sailed to Copenhagen and was gone from Hven for a month, pursuing his case against Gellius before the university court of Consistory. On the morning after Ash Wednesday, 25 February 1596, the appellate hearings opened in the medieval Consistory building; Tycho, accompanied by Dallin, Venusin and Carl Bryske, governor of Copenhagen Castle, declared he wanted no judgment, only a notarised public record, submitted the 16 January 1595 contract, and read into evidence a list of ten false rumours, standing to declare their authors liars. On 26 February Gellius pleaded illness and sent his brother David with power of attorney. The contemporary acts printed in Danske Magazin (1746) record these sessions and further proceedings in the Convent House; on 14 April 1596 the consistorium ruled on Tycho's preface, by which time some communications went by sent notes rather than appearance.

June 1596

BCopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1596b

In June 1596 Tycho was gone from Hven for nearly two weeks to attend the annual Diet of the nobility, which met to prepare the August coronation that would end the Regency. The great gathering assembled his brothers and kin at the peak of their oligarchic power: Steen Brahe on the Regency Council, Axel Brahe and Oluf Rosensparre admitted to the State Council that year, Jørgen and Knud Brahe holding the Varberg and Aarhus fiefs, cousin Steen Maltesen Sehested commanding Kronborg. His case against Gellius, however, was not ready in time for the Diet.

28 August 1596 – 9 September 1596

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1596e

Tycho left Hven from 28 August to 9 September 1596 to attend the coronation of Christian IV on 29 August, going with several famuli and wearing his golden chains with the Order of the Elephant and portrait medallions of two kings. His brother, Regent Steen Brahe, bore the royal orb; all four brothers played their parts and competed in the festive jousts while Tycho networked among the guests, including the Brandenburg court astronomer Johann Muller, who made a side-trip to Hven the day after Tycho's return, and the Scots ambassador Robert Anstruther, who also came on to Uraniborg. Bishop Peter Winstrup's sermon asserted that 'kings are gods' against the elective symbolism of the councillors' hands on the crown. Within a month the Nordfjord fief, at a thousand dalers his largest single revenue, was recalled.

A trip into Copenhagen four days after the signing of the Nordfjord transfer, in late September 1596, 'probably only confirmed Tycho's worst fears': the deaths of his protectors Kaas (1594) and Rosenkrantz (1596) had left an inner circle — the new chancellor Christian Friis foremost — philosophically committed to centralising crown revenue and at least somewhat hostile to him personally. The fief's recall dated 21 September 1596 was the first blow of the new reign.

The departure and exile

1597–159922 stays

The collapse and departure: the last Hven observation on 15 March 1597, the removal of the whole establishment to the Farvergade house in Copenhagen, the 2 June sailing into exile, the summer at Rostock, and the year as Rantzau's guest at Wandsbek, where the Mechanica was printed and the Elegia ad Daniam written. Then the interrupted first push toward Prague — Harburg, Magdeburg, a month at Dresden turned back by plague — and the Wittenberg winter in the Jessenius house until 14 June 1599. The itinerary's densest run of dated autographs and its hardest route reconciliations fall in these two years.

11 April 1597 – 2 June 1597

ACopenhagenstay-copenhagen-1597b

On Monday 11 April 1597 Tycho, Kirsten and the familia moved into the 'novum Museum Hafniense' — his own three-lot complex at the corner of Farvergade and Vestervold — with instruments on the rampart bastion granted him in 1589, the printing press and chemical laboratory in the house. The persecution peaked here: the pension had been stopped 18 March, and the assistants had already catalogued his books on Hven on 21 March; pastor Wensøsil, convicted at Roskilde 22 April, emerged from a month's dungeon to his shelter; the Hven peasants' charges were heard before the king; and in late May the town constable, on Lord Steward Walkendorf's orders, forbade him the bastion and city walls as an observatory. On 1 June he dismissed Longomontanus with a testimonial; on Thursday 2 June 1597 he left Copenhagen with a household of about twenty and every portable possession — instruments, laboratory, presses, books and papers — and never again set foot on Danish soil.
