Gassendi's hostile-commission and break-in details are Gassendi-only (grade C colour). The book cataloguing ('Registeret vi alle junkers bøger') stands under 21 March 1597 in the diary — on Hven, before the 11 April move; Christianson's weekday 'Saturday' for the 2 June departure is a slip (Thursday, Julian).

17 April 1597 – 20 April 1597

ARoskildestay-roskilde-1597
othersocial visitin transit
Tycho travelled to Roskilde on Sunday 17 April 1597 — the meteorological diary records 'Profectus est Tycho Roschyldiam' — into a stormy night and next-day blizzard, in the week of the church-ordinance prosecution of his Hven pastor Jens Jensen Wensøsil, tried before Bishop Peter Winstrup on Friday 22 April with the Kronborg commander Ditlev Holck sent to 'assist'. On Wednesday 20 April he met his brothers Steen and Axel Brahe, both state councillors, presumably concerting a defence. Wensøsil was convicted on both charges — omitting exorcism, and failing to punish Tycho, 'who for eighteen years has not taken Holy Eucharist but has lived an evil life with a mistress'. The real target was Tycho himself; he still held the prebend of the Holy Three Kings chapel there, lost on 10 June to the chancellor. The diary stops abruptly on 22 April 1597, never resumed.

June 1597

Ferried across the narrow straits to Falster, the exile party rode on through Nykøbing — seat of another royal castle formerly commanded by Tycho's foster father Jørgen Brahe, the second family landmark on the southbound road — before making for the port of Gedser at the island's southern tip. Like the other Danish road stations of June 1597, this is Christianson's reconstruction of the standard southern route rather than an independently documented halt; Tycho's presence on the road between Copenhagen (2 June) and Rostock (mid-June) is itself secure.

June 1597 – 8 September 1597

ARostockstay-rostock-1597
exilecourt & patronagepropertysocial visit
Tycho and his familia of about twenty settled into temporary quarters in Rostock around mid-June 1597, warmly received in his old student city — Chytraeus wrote a welcoming note on 16 June, and Lucas Bacmeister still kept the house of the 1566 duel. At St Mary's he took Holy Eucharist with his family for the first time in eighteen years. On 10 July he sent Christian IV the proud Danish-language letter defending his departure and offering to continue his work 'on fair conditions'; the crushing answer, dated 8 October, reached him only at Wandsbek. He sought Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg's intercession (late July), wrote Erik Sparre on 7 September about a Baltic island from King Sigismund, and lent the young Mecklenburg dukes 10,000 daler at 12 per cent, bond dated 24 August, secured on Amt Doberan — he had not left Denmark impoverished. Plague striking the town, he accepted Rantzau's Holstein invitation and left on 8 September 1597. Sent originals to Moritz of Hesse-Kassel (17 July) and Sparre (7 September) anchor presence.
Calendar. Julian. Arrival mid-June 1597 (month precision); departure day-dated 8 September 1597.

September 1597 – 8 October 1597 (bounds uncertain)

BBramstedtstay-bramstedt-1597a
court & patronagesocial visit
From Segeberg Tycho and the familia proceeded to Bramstedt, where Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau received them with open arms in the second half of September 1597. Host and guest, friends since Tycho's Rostock student days, talked over patronage strategy and a suitable residence until a Danish restoration could be won. Under the delicate protocol of status Rantzau would not become Tycho's patron nor Tycho his client; as friend and equal he offered, of the eighteen castles and manors he and his sons owned, Wandsburg near Hamburg, over the head of its lessee Georg Ludwig Frobenius, Tycho's old Hven acquaintance. Thoren has Tycho still (or again) at Bramstedt on 8 October 1597, talking over the alternatives when he sent a letter to Basel.

CDoberanstay-doberan-1597
in transitproperty
Leaving Rostock on 8 September 1597, the Brahe caravan proceeded westward through Doberan on the coastal road toward Wismar and Holstein — a pointed waypoint, since the whole Amt of Doberan had just been pledged as surety for Tycho's 10,000-daler loan to the young Mecklenburg dukes. Having refused to pay the sum out at Wismar, Tycho had offered to deliver it at Doberan in person, 'which probably happened' in Norlind's hedged wording; Friis, however, records only the promise, never the execution — and in 1601 it was Eske Bille and his servant, not Tycho, who travelled to Doberan and Rostock for the repayment. The passage is a named route stage in Christianson; no halt or business is independently documented.

17 September 1597

ASegebergstay-segeberg-1597
in transitcourt & patronageexile
By 17 September 1597 the exile party had reached Segeberg fortress, seat of Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau's administration of royal Schleswig-Holstein — one of the castles Rantzau had offered — only to find the viceroy away at Bramstedt. From Segeberg Tycho wrote him the dated letter (TBOO VIII,5) that fixes his presence: the castle pleased him, but he had left Hven to relocate, not retire — he had books to finish and needed typographic equipment, engravers and printers, so he asked for a residence near a city like Hamburg or Lübeck and offered to come to Bramstedt to discuss plans. That criterion shortly selected Wandsburg. Thoren's 'first estate, too remote for his taste', from which the 17 September letter was sent, is this same station, not a separate unnamed castle.

October 1597 – 29 September 1598

AWandsbekstay-wandsbek-1597
exilebooks & printingcourt & patronageobservationinstrumentsalchemy & medicine
A year as Rantzau's guest — not client — at the moated castle of Wandsburg in Wandsbek on Hamburg's outskirts, living in quasi-princely style, honoured at church in a special loge. Christian IV's rebuff of 8 October 1597 reached him here; on 20 October he entered the account of his interrupted observations and composed the Elegia ad Daniam, and on 21 October resumed observing, at first with only a radius, from February 1598 with quadrants, sextant and armilla (pole height 53°36'; lunar eclipse 10 February with Rosenkrantz assisting, solar eclipse 25 February, lunar 6 August). His own press from Hven, worked by the Hamburg printer Philipp von Ohr, produced the Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (dedication to Rudolf II dated 31 December 1597, ready early 1598), while copyists lettered vellum exemplars of the 1,000-star catalogue; both went out to princes and scholars across Europe as the patronage suit which, brokered by Rantzau, Hagecius, Corraducius and the Elector of Cologne, produced the imperial invitation in the summer. He kept a laboratory, shared medical recipes with Rantzau, answered Kepler's Mysterium on 1 April 1598, and received a stream of Danish students, Müller, Fabricius and, from August 1598, Longomontanus. Day-dated letters and album leaves run from 2 January to 14 September 1598. Just after Michaelmas, 29 September 1598, the caravan rolled out toward the Elbe road.
Calendar. Julian. Arrival month-level only: late September (Christianson) or mid-October 1597 (Dreyer, Thoren, Friis, Björklund); departure day-dated 29 September 1598.

22 December 1597

ABramstedtstay-bramstedt-1597b
court & patronagesocial visit
Viceroy Rantzau arranged for Tycho to meet Margrave Joachim Frederick of Brandenburg and Margravine Catherine of Brandenburg-Küstrin at Bramstedt on 22 December 1597, as the parents of Christian IV's bride returned home through Holstein from the royal wedding (Haderslev, 27 November). Tycho handed the margrave a letter and memorandum of his reasons for leaving Denmark, seeking intercession with his new royal son-in-law — either the permanent endowment of Uraniborg or leave to remove the four great instruments with compensation. The accommodating couple's letters to king and queen of January–February 1598 (25 January and days following) led to nothing. The meeting also renewed acquaintance with the Brandenburg court astrologer Johannes Müller, who had visited Hven in 1596 and would shortly join Tycho at Wandsbek.

October 1598 – December 1598 (bounds uncertain)

ADresdenstay-dresden-1598
in transitcourt & patronage
Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a small suite spent about a month in the Electoral Saxon residence city (late October to the first days of December 1598). He announced his approach to the imperial court through Vice-Chancellor Corraducius; the round trip of the inquiry took a month, Prague being gripped by plague and Rudolf withdrawn (to Pilsen, per Björklund's Bilag 4). Secretary Barvitius's reply — the emperor was pleased he was on the way but he should wait at a safe distance — turned him to wintering at Wittenberg. In Dresden he had an audience with Duke Frederick William of Saxe-Altenburg, administrator of Electoral Saxony, presenting illuminated copies of the Mechanica and star catalogue to the duke, the boy Elector Christian II and Chancellor Mosbach, and receiving a golden chain with three portrait medallions worth over 130 gulden. From Dresden on 28 November 1598 he dated the letter to the Doge of Venice — carried by Tengnagel across the Alps, proposing among other things the affiliate observatory at Alexandria — and wrote Magini after a seven-year silence. His son Tycho was sent back to Wandsbek to fetch the family.
Calendar. Day-dated anchors: Waller album leaf, Dresden 10 November; son Tyge's album entry 27 November; letters to the Doge of Venice and Magini 28 November 1598.

October 1598

AMagdeburgstay-magdeburg-1598
in transitcourt & patronagepropertysocial visit
The caravan progressed up the Elbe to Magdeburg and halted about eight days in October 1598. Tycho met his long-time correspondent Rector Georg Rollenhagen — source of the first warnings of Ursus's plagiarism and of imperial-court intelligence via Caspar Lehmann, including the rumour that Rudolf meant to grant him Brandeis castle. Erik Lange, Sophie Brahe's absconded betrothed, turned up: Tycho barred him and his gold-making schemes from the Prague party, but before a summoned notary required his sworn public testimony on Ursus's 1584 conduct at Uraniborg — ammunition for the plagiarism war. Strategy changed here: the heavy instruments and baggage were stored at Magdeburg (they stayed until 1600), and Longomontanus escorted Kirsten and the daughters back to Wandsburg — prospects being too uncertain to drag the whole household on — while Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a few others pressed on toward Dresden.

5 October 1598

AHarburgstay-harburg-1598
in transitcourt & patronage
First call of the Prague journey: the caravan — three splendid carriages, Tycho's drawn by six horses, out of Wandsburg just after Michaelmas — crossed to the ducal seat of Harburg on the Elbe's south bank, where Tycho paid his respects to the aged Duke Otto II of Braunschweig-Lüneburg, whose daughter Duchess Elisabeth was married to Tycho's Swedish kinsman Count Erik Brahe. He presented an illuminated copy of the Mechanica bound in green silk, inscribed 5 October 1598; the fascinated duke asked for his nativity and reciprocated with a letter of recommendation to the imperial High Steward Wolfgang Rumpf — a document Tycho would produce at his Prague audience the next summer, alongside the commendations of Elector Ernest and Duke Ulrich.

25 October 1598

AWittenbergstay-wittenberg-1598a
in transit
A dated album leaf — 'Suspiciendo despicio', Tycho's personal device (Sotheby's Paris, 15 December 2004, lot 36) — places him bodily at Wittenberg on 25 October 1598, between the Magdeburg week and the Dresden month. The Elbe road from Magdeburg to Dresden passed through Wittenberg, where, per Thoren, the Jessenius acquaintance was first made in passing; the leaf is therefore read as a transit attestation on the outward leg, not the start of the winter residence, which the biographies date from 4 December. A candidate host album, Johann Nesen's Stammbuch (Zittau, Christian-Weise-Bibliothek B 178, the Tycho leaf excised), records the entry under 26 October 1598 — a one-day discrepancy unresolved. An undated 1598 Wittenberg entry now trimmed into the Merseburg autograph collection belongs either to this passage or to the December residence.

4 December 1598 – 14 June 1599

AWittenbergstay-wittenberg-1598b
exileeducationbooks & printingobservationalchemy & medicinesocial visit
Tycho and his sons arrived in Wittenberg on 4 December 1598 and lodged with the anatomist Johannes Jessenius (Jan Jesenský) in Philipp Melanchthon's former house — later Caspar Peucer's, known to Tycho from his 1566 student days. He set up a chemical laboratory on the ground floor, observed the sun's meridian altitude on 9 December, and gathered a circle including the mathematician Melchior Jöstelius (who perfected prosthaphaeresis with him), the theologian Ägidius Hunnius and the poet Friedrich Taubmann. The total lunar eclipse of 31 January 1599 ran nearly half an hour against his lunar theory, halting the Progymnasmata Moon-section printing for recalculation — a manuscript ephemeris for 1599 was substituted as imperial gift. In February 1599, never before formally matriculated, he enrolled with his sons and famulus Johannes Eriksen; the rector feted him at the castle. Kirsten and the daughters, from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January. Coraduz's summons matured through the spring, but carriage horses, Magdalene's grave illness, thaw and floods delayed departure until 14 June 1599 — the farewell album leaf 'quo Witebergā discessi'. The densest dated-autograph run of his life spans the stay: 14 January (Hagecius Mechanica dedication), 28 February (his son's album), 6 March (Sinnich), 16 April (the Palingenius leaf, Sophia stock 6196), 8 and 29 May.
Calendar. Departure 14 June 1599 expressly old style (Julian) — Norlind from Tycho's note in his Apianus ('g.st.'); Thoren argues the same from the Wittenberg context and 'right after summer solstice'.

The sources disagree. Arrival: 4 December 1598 (Christianson p. 302, Norlind p. 298; Dreyer 'first week of December') vs an earlier back-calculation of this edition (c. 21 October, from a 236-day figure) and Nielsen's 'October 1598' interlude start — 4 December followed, the 25 October leaf read as an en-route touch. Departure: 'at Easter 1599' (Nielsen; Dreyer and Friis 'shortly after Easter'; Gassendi 'not before Easter, for the floods') vs the dated leaves of 16 April, 8 and 29 May and the 14 June 1599 farewell self-dating (Christianson, Norlind) — 14 June governs. Length: Jessenius's funeral oration says nine months; the documented span is about six and a half; the 236-day figure of that earlier reading (implying an October arrival) is unexplained. Cause of the halt: plague at Prague and the scattered court (all biographies, Gassendi, Jönsson) vs Šíma-Valeška's express rejection of the plague explanation — the plague account is far better attested but the objection is flagged. Calendar of 14 June: Thoren 'corrects Norlind' toward old style, yet Norlind's own text prints '14 juni 1599 g.st.' — a discrepancy of transcription, both in fact Julian. Family logistics: women from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January (Christianson) vs Dreyer's 'escorted by Longomontanus as far as Magdeburg, joined during the winter' vs Friis's separate route 'via Magdeburg to Dresden'. Dreyer additionally has the post-Easter departure leave the family 'half way, at Dresden' — against Christianson's 14 June departure 'with all his familia'; the day-dated leaf governs, the Dresden family-parking belongs, if real, to the 1599 journey.

Bohemia

1599–160115 stays

Summoned by Rudolf II, Tycho left Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 and travelled via Pretzsch and Dresden to Prague, where a wholly private imperial audience made him court astronomer at 3,000 gulden a year. Choosing Benátky nad Jizerou over Brandeis and Lysá, he built his last observatory there from August 1599, received Kepler in February 1600, and fled plague to Girsitz over the winter. Recalled to Prague in June 1600, he lodged at the Golden Griffin, set his twenty-eight instruments up at the Belvedere, and moved into the Curtius house in February 1601. The Rožmberk banquet of 13 October 1601 began the fatal illness; he died on 24 October and was buried in the Týn Church on 4 November.

June 1599 – August 1599

APraguestay-prague-1599
court & patronageexileobservationinstruments
Arrival in Bohemia and the making of the imperial appointment. Reaching Prague in late June or the first days of July 1599 — Ursus fleeing the city at his approach — Tycho was greeted by the privy secretary Barvitius, received by High Steward Rumpf in long Latin conversation, and granted a wholly private audience by Rudolf II, who took his hand, accepted the three presentation volumes (the Mechanica, the vellum star catalogue, the sun-and-moon theory) and promised 3,000 gulden yearly with a hereditary fief to follow. He was lodged in the late vice-chancellor Curtius's house on Hradčany, where a painted pedestal in the Uraniborg manner was built; he signed the von Wicken album at Prague on 13 July; he observed the 22 July solar eclipse with his own instruments while his assistant watched from the Carolinum tower, and his Prague solar series ends 31 July. Finding the Curtius tower too small and dreading visitors, he asked for a country seat and was offered three castles.
Calendar. Bohemia used the Gregorian calendar. Dreyer has Tycho adopting new style from Prague onward (the 22 July 1599 eclipse date is n.s.); Thoren notes his 30 August 1599 letter to Rosenkrantz still dated old style.

14 June 1599 – 15 June 1599

APretzschstay-pretzsch-1599
in transitsocial visit
First halt of the definitive move to Bohemia. Leaving Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 with the whole familia — a train of wagons, carriages and outriders — Tycho spent the first evening at Castle Pretzsch on the Elbe as guest of the Saxon hereditary marshal Johann (Hans) Löser, a courtesy the recently money-humbled astronomer thought worth recording for Rosenkrantz. The party continued upriver toward Dresden the next day.
Calendar. Saxony kept the Julian calendar: 14–16 June 1599 o.s. = 24–26 June n.s.; the Bohemian dates that follow are new style.

16 June 1599 (departure within the month)

ADresdenstay-dresden-1599
in transitfamily
The Dresden split of the household. Arriving on 16 June 1599, two days out of Wittenberg, Tycho left Kirsten, the daughters and their servants in the care of Johann Tauchmann, a high Saxon court official and brother-in-law of his Wittenberg collaborator Jöstelius, and went on toward Prague in his finest carriage with his sons and Claus Mule — a deliberate strategy of appearing before the emperor unencumbered, and of holding a line of retreat. On imperial instructions after the first audience the family was fetched, reaching Prague eight days after being sent for.
Calendar. Saxony kept the Julian calendar: 14–16 June 1599 o.s. = 24–26 June n.s.; the Bohemian dates that follow are new style.

20 August 1599 – June 1600 (bounds uncertain)

ABenátky nad Jizerou · Benátky nad Jizerou — Tycho's first Bohemian observatory →stay-benatky-1599
observationinstrumentsalchemy & medicinecourt & patronagefamilyproperty
The last observatory. Choosing Benátky nad Jizerou — highest of the three offered crown estates, c. 35 km northeast of Prague above the 'Venice of Bohemia' — Tycho arrived about 20–21 August 1599, had his first instrument mounted by 28 August, and set about remodelling the castle into a new Uraniborg with observatory and chymical laboratory, against the obstruction of the administrator Mühlstein and an empty treasury (imperial resolution of 10 December 1599: 1,000 gulden yearly from the Brandeis-Benátky rents). His first recorded observation there is 11 September 1599; datelines run 'from the imperial castle Benatky' from 7 September 1599 to 15 May 1600. Son Tycho and Claus Mule fetched the great instruments from Denmark; Longomontanus rejoined in January 1600 for the lunar theory; Kepler first met him here on 3 February 1600 and was set to Mars, the contract quarrel mediated by Jessenius on 5 April. David Gans came thrice from Prague, five days each. Observations break off at the end of June 1600, when the emperor recalled him to Prague.
Calendar. Datelines from Bohemia are new style — Tycho says so expressly in the 22 March 1600 letter ('epther denne Ny Stil'). Arrival is bracketed by the Brandeis letter of 20 August 1599 and the first instrument set up by 28 August; departure by the end of the observation series (end of June 1600, Studnicka) against Norlind's early July and Dreyer's c. August.

The sources disagree. Departure for Prague: observations end at the end of June 1600 (Studnicka; Christianson 2020 has the household leave after Rudolf's 10 June return) vs early July (Norlind) vs c. August on Barvitius's advice (Dreyer); June followed as the modern consensus, with Friis's dateline gap (15 May 1600 Benátky — 26 September 1600 Prague) bracketing it. Kepler's arrival: 3 February 1600 (Dreyer, McEvoy in Crossroads) vs 4 February summons (Christianson 2020) vs 'January to Prague' (Jönsson, outlier) — 3 February followed. Longomontanus's discharge: 18 July 1600 at Benátky (Christianson 2000) vs 4 August / August 1600 (Christianson 2020, Friis, Norlind, Dreyer). The Hamburg-senate letter's two internal datings (29 September 1599 slug vs '27 jan. n.s. Benatky') disagree; both place Tycho at Benátky in 1599–1600. Jönsson places Benátky 'southwest' of Prague — a geographical error; the castle lies northeast.

20 August 1599 – 21 August 1599

ABrandýs nad Labemstay-brandys-1599
in transitproperty
Seen on the castle-selection circuit and passed over — sitting low, the Emperor's favourite hunting-lodge — Brandeis nonetheless anchors the removal to Benátky: on the way there Tycho datelined a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock from Brandeis, 20 August 1599 (new style), reporting a level road about six hours from Prague and that an official of Brandeis would carry him and all his effects to Benátky that day or the next. Brandeis remained the administrative seat, under Kaspar von Mühlstein, from which his Benátky building funds were grudgingly managed. He never resided here.
Calendar. Friis expressly flags the 20 August 1599 dateline as new style.

November 1599 – January 1600

BGirsitz (Jičice?)stay-girsitz-1599
otherobservationin transit
Plague refuge. After two thousand deaths in the Benátky district — a travelling companion of the visiting cousin Claus Steensen Bille sickened and died on arrival — Tycho took the frightened household to the castle of Girsitz in the first half of November 1599. He said they stayed six or seven weeks: his first letter from Girsitz is of 16 November, the last officially sent from there of 31 December 1599, with the return to Benátky in the new year; some intervening letters were addressed from Benátky 'just to avoid complicating things', so the exact return is unfixable. Some observations were made in December, and during this visitation the Emperor asked Tycho for the prescription of his elixir against epidemic diseases.

c. April 1600

BPraguestay-prague-1600b
social visitin transit
The Kepler reconciliation. About three weeks after Kepler's angry departure from Benátky on 6 April 1600 and his withdrawal to Baron Hoffmann's house in Prague, Hoffmann's and Jessenius's mediation and Kepler's repentant letter brought the two astronomers together at Prague: Tycho drove into the city — something he had told Kepler he did not like to do — was reconciled with his errant assistant, and fetched him back to Benátky, where Kepler worked a further four weeks before leaving for Graz at the beginning of June.

c. 1 May 1600

APraguestay-prague-1600c
social visit
At the beginning of May 1600, while resident at Benátky, Tycho attended Caspar von Mühlstein's wedding in Prague — a sign of cordial relations with the estates' captain after the December 1599 settlement of their funding frictions. Tycho's own letter of 15 May 1600 dates it: 'wie ich fur 14 tage zu Prage, auf des Herrn Haubtmans von Brandeis Hochzeit gewesen'. In this period he grew acquainted with Protestant aristocrats including Baron Ehrenfried von Minckwitz, who blazoned the same arms as his Ulfstand grandmother, and Baron Siegfried von Rindscheid, the alchemist who had visited Uraniborg with Erik Lange in 1584.

June 1600 – 24 October 1601 (bounds uncertain)

APraguestay-prague-1600
court & patronageobservationbooks & printingfamilyinstrumentsdeath & burial
The final residence. Summoned when Rudolf II returned from Pilsen on 10 June 1600, Tycho moved to Prague suddenly and permanently: first weeks in the noisy Golden Griffin inn on Nový Svět below the castle (twice summoned to the palace in one day), then a private house near Baron Hoffmann's by the Loreto square. The twenty-eight instruments — from Benátky, and the great ones from Hven via the Magdeburg transit dispute — arrived by October-November 1600 and were installed at the Belvedere; the press resumed the Progymnasmata; Jacob Monaw brought the Wittich library's annotated De revolutionibus copies in October 1600, and Kepler, expelled from Styria, returned destitute on 19 October 1600 and was set to refuting Ursus. On 25 February 1601 the household moved into the Curtius house, bought by the emperor. Elisabeth married Tengnagel on 17 June 1601; in September 1601 Tycho presented Kepler to the emperor and the Tabulae Rudolphinae were named. His last observation is dated 11 October 1601; the Rožmberk banquet of 13 October began the fatal illness, and he died at home on 24 October 1601, aged 54 years 10 months, charging Kepler to complete the tables in the Tychonic scheme.
Calendar. All Bohemian dates new style (Gregorian, used in Bohemia from 1584). Death 24 October 1601 n.s.; the older literature's '13 October old style' conflates the banquet date, and Kepler's '24 November' in the Rudolphine Tables preface is a slip refuted at length by Gassendi.

The sources disagree. Start of the permanent Prague residence: June 1600 on Rudolf's 10 June return (Thoren, Christianson 2000/2020, Jönsson) vs 'about the beginning of July' (Norlind, from the 3 August postscript 'called a month ago') vs 'about August' (Dreyer) — June followed (modern consensus); Friis's datelines bracket it 15 May – 26 September 1600, his 26 July 'In eil, Prag' letter possibly the move itself. Death date: 24 October 1601 unanimous against Kepler's '24 November' slip (Gassendi's refutation) and the older '13 October old style' (Studnicka's correction: 13 October n.s. is the banquet). Time of death: 'around nine that evening' (Christianson 2020) vs 'between nine and ten in the forenoon' (Jönsson) vs morning (Friis, Dreyer) — morning better attested. Elisabeth's wedding: 17 June 1601 (Thoren, Jönsson, Christianson) vs Friis's 'between Easter and Pentecost 1601'. Cause of death: uraemia from prostatic hypertrophy (Norlind; modern opinion per Thoren; Christianson via Jessenius) vs the contemporary stone attribution (Wittich; no stones found at exhumation); mercury poisoning is excluded by the 2010 exhumation and uraemia is consistent but unproven — Christianson 2000's 'body heavy with quicksilver from Paracelsian elixirs' is not carried as fact. Norlind judges the Capuchin-protocol account of Tycho's court role 'extremely tendentious and certainly historically false in most points'.

2 December 1600 – February 1601 (bounds uncertain)

BPrague · The Belvedere (Royal Summer Palace) — Tycho's Prague Musaeum →stay-prague-1600d
observationinstruments
Surrogate Uraniborg. In the Royal Summer Palace of Queen Anna — the Belvedere, 'non longe ab Arce in Caesaris quadam magnifice exstructa domo' in Tycho's report of 24 January 1601 — his twenty-eight instruments, arrived in Prague in October–November 1600 (Thoren: sometime in October, a few weeks after the Magdeburg consignment), were stored and mounted on the second-storey porch, and on 2 December 1600 the observations broken off at Benátky at the end of June were resumed; by Christmas night Tycho was observing. Pierre Bergeron (1607) records that the great Danish mathematician made his precise observations in the ground-floor arcaded galleries — reported rather than firmly documented for Tycho's own person. After his death the building housed the astronomical section of Rudolf's collections, a memorial musaeum with two portraits of Tycho.
Calendar. Observations resumed at the Belvedere on 2 December 1600 (Studnicka); it served until the Curtius house was fully adapted; Tycho's report of 24 January 1601 describes the establishment.

The sources disagree. Tycho's personal observing in the Belvedere arcades rests on Pierre Bergeron (1607) and the site record grades it 'reported, not firmly documented'; the resumption of the observation series there on 2 December 1600 is documentary (Studnicka), and Thoren has Tycho himself observing by Christmas night 1600.

25 February 1601 – 24 October 1601

APrague · The Curtius (Kurtz) house — Tycho's Prague residence and place of death →stay-prague-1601
court & patronageobservationfamilydeath & burial
Last workplace and deathplace. On 25 February 1601 the familia moved into the refurbished summer palace of the late vice-chancellor Jacob Kurz von Senftenau (Curtius) on Hradčany, bought by the emperor for 10,000 thaler and transformed toward a 'New Imperial Uraniborg'; observing resumed there on 3 March 1601, seven teams having taken the solar culmination simultaneously on 28 February. Elisabeth Brahe married Tengnagel in the house in June 1601; the Pruskowski Mechanica dedication of 12 March 1601, among the latest securely-dated Tycho autographs, was signed in this residence. After the banquet of 13 October Tycho returned here unable to pass water and died on 24 October 1601, Kirsten, Kepler and the household about him, Longomontanus and Tengnagel far from Prague. The Bohemian royal astronomer Alois David fixed the observation tower's coordinates in 1803; the structure was demolished in 1804.
Calendar. Move-in 25 February 1601 (Dreyer, Friis, Christianson 2020) against Norlind's 23 February at dawn; death 24 October 1601, all new style.

13 October 1601

APrague · The Schwarzenberg (Rožmberk) palace — Tycho's last banquet →stay-prague-1601b
social visit
The fatal banquet. On 13 October 1601 Tycho went with the councillor Ehrenfried von Minckwitz to dine at the palace of Petr Vok z Rožmberka — by Thoren's reckoning (Appendix 5) the Renaissance palace on Hradčany square later known as the Schwarzenberg palace — a magnate of his bookish Prague circle, owner of some 10,000 books and manuscripts. Forbearing, as manners required while his host remained at table, to rise and relieve himself, he held his urine too long; by the time he returned home he could not urinate, and the eleven-day fatal illness began. The retention story is the contemporary tradition transmitted by Kepler's log and the funeral oration, not an established medical fact.
Calendar. 13 October 1601, new style (Bohemia was Gregorian); the same date read as old style generated the erroneous '13 October' death date in the older literature.

The sources disagree. The banquet itself, its date and Tycho's presence are unanimous.

4 November 1601

APrague · Church of Our Lady before Týn — Tycho's grave →stay-prague-1601c
death & burial
The burial. On 4 November 1601 a solemn procession bore the coffin — velvet-covered, hung with his ancestors' gilded arms, preceded by the black damask banner with his title, his led horse and gilt rapier — across the Charles Bridge along the royal way to the Church of Our Lady before Týn in the Old Town, where the utraquist rite still allowed a Protestant service. Twelve noble imperial guardsmen carried him; his younger son Jørgen walked between Count Erik Brahe and Baron von Minckwitz, the widow following; the eldest son and son-in-law Tengnagel were abroad. Jessenius delivered the funeral oration, printed at Prague the same year. The red Slivenec marble monument — armoured effigy, hand on the celestial globe, 'NON FASCES, NEC OPES, SOLA ARTIS SCEPTRA PERENNANT' — still marks the tomb, where Kirsten was laid beside him in 1604. (This final entry records the burial rite of 4 November — Tycho died on 24 October; it closes the itinerary as the body's last journey, not a living presence.)
Calendar. Gregorian (Bohemia).

The sources disagree. The two prague-bohemia witnesses do not themselves date the funeral day; 4 November 1601 rests on the wider tradition (Danske Magazin 1746, Dreyer, Friis, Christianson, Norlind, Jönsson) and is unanimous there. The grave's afterlife (1901 and 2010 exhumations) is out of scope for the itinerary.

4The gazetteer and the life-map

The gazetteer holds one record per location, with its modern name, the forms under which the period sources name it, its coordinates and — equally — where those coordinates came from. Nine records carry no stay; each is a place the compilation needed for a reason the record states, and §11 accounts for all nine. Twelve carry no pin, either because the source names a region rather than a locality or because it names no place that can be identified; these never appear on the map, and saying so is more useful than guessing.

5The sites

The places are where he was; these are what he built, and what became of it. Fourteen structures are recorded — the island establishment on Hven and the Bohemian dwellings of the exile — each with its date, its survival status, the rooms it contained and the instruments they housed, its fate, and, where one exists, a link to the thing itself. For Uraniborg and Stjerneborg the primary architectural record is Charles Christensen's measured reconstruction of 1921, printed here with its excavation evidence, its dimension comparison and the surviving relics; Blaeu's much-reproduced views are given beneath it as the inherited print tradition they are, schematic and unreliable in detail.

Uraniborg,
explored Imagines — how Uraniborg was pictured → Every depiction printed in Tycho’s lifetime, graded for reliability — and the measured reconstruction (Beckett & Christensen, 1921) that corrects them. Geometria — how the plan was constructed → How one square and one circle generate house, gardens and ramparts, step by step. Diarium — the island’s visitor register → Who came to Hven 1586–1597, day by day — and when Tycho himself was away.

Hven — the island establishment 9 sites

Hven (Ven) — the island fief

extantA1576–1597 · Ven (Hven)site-hven
The island of Hven (Swedish Ven) in the Øresund, granted to Tycho as a fief by Frederik II on 23 May 1576 — rent-free for as long as he lived and continued his mathematical studies, with 400 daler from the treasury toward a house he was to build on the island (Tycho himself supplying the stone and lime; Kancelliets Brevbøger 1576–79 p. 59). Today part of Sweden (Landskrona kommun). In his own words, “The island itself is very high, as if it were a mountain which you might ascend, but on top it is flat all over”; it lies in the Sound “which divides Scania from Sealand,” with Copenhagen three miles to the south-west, and its “latitude from the equator is 55°54½′, as measured several times by us with the greatest care” (Mechanica, trans. Ræder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, pp. 138–139). Tycho's two decades on Hven were also a hard landlordship. He held the island's tenants to heavy labour-service on Uraniborg and its works, and his disputes with them — and with the Crown over their grievances — run through the record: a royal letter of 1587 and another of 1592 document the friction, the latter in the matter of his tenant Rasmus Pedersen of Gundsømagle, whom Tycho had barred from a farm and had imprisoned, the King directing that the suit be heard before the landsdommer Lauge Beck (Becker, Danske Magazin 3. R. IV–V). Even from his Wandsbek exile Tycho went on managing the island at a distance — a Danish letter of 28 May 1598 thanks the Lord High Steward Christoffer Valkendorf for backing his bailiff against the 'disobedient peasants' there (Epistolarium: Tycho to Christoffer Valkendorf, 28 May 1598). The tenants' grievances were among the grounds on which Tycho lost royal favour and, in 1597, the fief itself. The chancery records document the friction in detail: as early as 1578 the Crown forbade Hven's tenants to move off the island without Tycho's leave 'medens han bygger der paa Landet' (KB 1576–79 p. 334); on the tenants' complaint of intolerable labour-service the King sent Arild Ugerup and Axel Gyldenstierne to Hven (20 August 1580), whose report produced the formal 'Ordning og Skik mellem Tyge Brahe og Bønderne paa Hven' of 8 January 1581 — two days' labour-service a week per half-farm, the tenants' claimed freeholder (jordegne) status revoked, and Hven's court cases moved to the Skaane landsting (KB 1580–83 pp. 128–129, 200-201). Tycho's Crown income beyond Hven was itself a knot of fiefs: Kullegaarden on the Kullen peninsula in Skaane (granted 1577), which carried the duty of keeping the Kullen lighthouse 'i Stand og lade den blusse den sædvanlige Tid' and, as Tycho successfully argued in 1579, supplied the firewood for Uraniborg (KB 1576–79 pp. 230, 249, 765; 1580–83 pp. 294–295); the prebend of the Helligtrekongers Kapel in Roskilde Cathedral (held 1579–1597, with jus patronatus over Udbye parish); the Norwegian fief of Nordfjord (1578), exchanged in 1586 for 400 daler yearly from the Øresund toll; and a royal pension terminated in 1581 once the fiefs sufficed. The end came together: a fresh royal commission investigated the tenants' renewed grievances on 9 April 1597, and in June 1597 the Roskilde prebend passed to Chancellor Christen Friis 'saaledes som Tyge Brahe hidtil har haft det' (KB 1596–1602 pp. 113, 168, 170) in the same weeks Tycho gave up Hven. The island passed in 1602 to a new lensmand, Cort Barleben, on ordinary commercial terms (50 daler the first year, 100 thereafter), by which time the buildings were reported 'meget forfalden' (KB 1596–1602 pp. 739, 746).
Dimensions. highest in the middle and flat on top; latitude 55°54½′ (Tycho's own determination); circumference 8160 passus (Mechanica 1946, pp. 138–139)
See it
The building stands, but no stable institutional record has been verified for it here.

Between Zealand and Scania lies in the Sound a small island, called Hven, or Venusia, so named by Tycho Brahe, who laboured there for more than twenty-two years over astronomy.

Dutch original

Tusschen Zeelandt en Schonen legt in de Sond een klijn Eylandt, genomende Hven, ofte Venusia, só genaamt van Tycho Brahe, die daer meer als tweentwintig jaren over de Stelkunde heeft gearbeyt.

Joan Blaeu, Grooten Atlas oft Werelt-beschryving (Amsterdam, 1664), p. 174. Universiteitsbibliotheek Utrecht, AC 62 Rariora.

Uraniborg — the castle of the heavens

ruinedA1576–1580 · Ven (Hven)site-uraniborg
Tycho's great house, built 1576–1580 ön a square rampart-enclosed plot whose four corners pointed to the compass points, with four roads running from those corners to the raised circular space at the centre where the house stood. The central building was a square 49 feet ön a side, with round towers 18 feet in diameter ön its north and south faces (ringed by lower outhouses för fuel) and narrow entrance towers east and west; it was built apparently of red brick with sandstone ornaments in the 'Gothic Renaissance' style then new to the North — epoch-making, Dreyer judged, in the history of Scandinavian architecture. A single building uniting residence, library and upper observatory galleries above än alchemical laboratory in the basement. Its artistic genesis is still debated — advisers proposed from Hans van Paeschen (first builder of Kronborg) to the royal sculptor Johan Gregor van der Schardt — but the 1587 tablet in the great mural-quadrant painting names Tycho himself 'the constructor of the buildings and the astronomical instruments', and the domed-centre-in-a-geometric-garden plan shows a strong affinity with Italian villa architecture, especially Palladio's Villa Rotonda (Johannsen, in Tycho Brahes Verden, 2006). The standard art-historical monograph ön the building — Jern's Uraniborg: herresäte och himlaborg (Lund, 1976) — locates the specific model för the gabled façade not in the villa tradition but in Venetian church fronts, comparing it directly with S. Giovanni in Bragora and S. Maria della Carità, while cautioning that Uraniborg cannot be reduced to any single Renaissance style-circle (Jern 1976). The documented hands are these: the Netherlandish master-builder Hans von Paschen led the work before transferring to Bohus in 1577; Hans van Stenwinkel the Elder completed the interior and built Stjerneborg (royal architect, 1582); the Nuremberg founder Georg Labenwolf laid the lead-pipe water system and fountain; and Tobias Gemperlin painted the great mural quadrant (Jern 1976). Over its two doors Tycho set paired mottoes that made the building's double programme explicit — Suspiciendo despicio ('by looking up I look down') över the eastern, astronomical portal, and Despiciendo suspicio ('by looking down I look up') över the western, alchemical one — so that astronomy and the laboratory's 'terrestrial astronomy' answered each other across the house (Jern 1976). In his own words, Tycho chose “the site highest ön this island … practically in its centre, where I started building from its foundations a castle which was named after the heaven itself in which it was its task to make observations, and hence called Uraniborg.” He gives the rampart-square as three hundred feet ön a side, the central house as “nearly sixty feet” per side under a forty-five-foot wall, and seventy-five feet “from the ground to the Pegasus at the very top” (Mechanica, trans. Ræder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 126). These figures are in Tycho's short foot of 259 mm, so the house is ≈15.5 m square — consistent with the 49-foot figure (in the larger Danish foot) recorded above.
Dimensions. central building a square of 49 feet per side; round towers 18 feet in diameter on the north and south sides; narrow entrance towers east and west (Dreyer, p. 96, from Tycho's own Epistolae astronomicae p. 218 + Mechanica fol. H.4)
Fate. decay documented from Tycho's departure — royal commissioners Thomas Fincke and Iver Stub were sent on 2 June 1597 to inspect the damage the Hven tenants had done to the instruments still on Uraniborg (KB 1596–1602 p. 163); by June 1602 the buildings were reported 'meget forfalden' and surveyed for the new lensmand Cort Barleben (KB p. 746). Demolished and quarried in the 17th century; only foundations survive, partly restored

Measured reconstruction — Christensen 1921the primary architectural record
Charles Christensen's measured reconstruction (1921) is the authoritative modern record of how Uraniborg actually looked. It rests on C. V. L. Charlier's 1901 excavation of the foundations, collated against — and correcting — every depiction printed in Tycho's own lifetime.

Excavation. C. V. L. Charlier excavated the foundations in 1901. The recovered ground-plan does not agree with the plans Tycho himself printed (which are wrong “end ikke i de store Hovedtræk” — not even in the main outlines); the reconstruction therefore follows the excavated measurements, not the printed figures.

The printed sources disagree on almost every dimension; the reconstruction uses the excavated measurements. Feet are Tychonic feet.
Surviving relics
• Foundation-stone fragment (porphyry, with Charles Dançay's Latin inscription; the stone reads 1 August, where the Mechanica gives 8 August 1576) — Lund University Historical Museum (Fig. 1)
• Window-crown fragment (volute-crowned, the motif peculiar to Uraniborg) — Lund University Historical Museum (Fig. 5)
• Two Arion-on-a-dolphin bronze water-taps from the piped water system — Lund University Historical Museum (Fig. 26)
Design source. The design adapts Palladio's Villa Rotonda (known via the engraving in I quattro libri dell'architettura, 1570): Uraniborg keeps the square plan and the four axial corridors but drops the central circular domed hall (impractical in a Nordic house), substitutes octagonal portal-projections for the open loggias, and adds the two round towers N and S. Vitruvian symmetria — invoked by Tycho in the Mechanica's description of the east front, after the architectural learning he had professed since his 1574 oration — governs the whole; the volute window-crowns follow Serlio, the timber cupola Walter Rivius's German Vitruvius (1548). [Jern 1976 later relocates the façade source from the Veneto villa to Venetian church fronts — a competing attribution.]

Basement
The great alchemical laboratory. Sixteen furnaces of nine kinds in the south projection; one furnace-base was recovered in the 1901 excavation.
The well cellar. The masonry well (about 40 alen deep) under the north tower that fed the pressurised water system; still extant.
Ground floor
The central crossing and fountain. Where the four axial corridors meet, with a water-spouting Vandkunst at the centre.
Vinterstue (the winter room). The family living-room (SE); later enlarged, with a hidden five-furnace spagyric laboratory built behind its chimney.
The mural-quadrant room. The SW ground-floor room: the great brass mural quadrant on the meridian wall (its west window blinded, a slit cut in the south wall), and above the arc the 1587 trompe-l'oeil wall-painting of Tycho in effigy.
Quadrans muralis sive Tichonicus — the great mural quadrant
The guest rooms. Two further ground-floor chambers, each with a fireplace and beds; the NE one opened to the kitchen.
The kitchen. In the north tower, around the masonry well.

The gardens and ramparts of Uraniborg

reconstructedB1576; redesigned after 1590 · Ven (Hven)site-gardens
The square earthwork ramparts enclosing Uraniborg, their corners set to the cardinal points, with formal gardens and orchards within and around them — among the finest in Scandinavia by Tycho's own account. Christianson describes the orchard's pippin, Rambour and Gylling apples, Doyenné and blood pears, green and blue Reine Claude plums, morello cherries, apricots, figs, quince and walnuts, and knot gardens laid out as a microcosm; Tycho's sister Sophie Brahe is recorded helping lay out and replant the garden (boxwood cuttings noted in his diary). Tycho rebuilt the ramparts and redesigned and replanted the knot gardens and orchards in the renovations of c.1591. Beyond its beauty the garden carried a symbolic-alchemical programme (Michelsen, in Tycho Brahes Verden, 2006): the medicinal plants were set in precisely planned beds so as to absorb the maximum heavenly influence (a Paracelsian-medicine principle), the enclosed garden read as a microcosm of the cosmic order and a figure of the Opus Magnum — one of the main elements of Tycho's 'earthly chemistry', in harmony with the astronomy pursued in Urania's house at its centre.
Fate. lost; the geometry recovered by excavation and partly recreated on site

The alchemical laboratory

lostB1580 · Ven (Hven)site-laboratory
The alchemical laboratory in Uraniborg's basement, fitted with sixteen furnaces of nine different kinds — Tycho's 'terrestrial astronomy', where he prepared medicines (the plague elixirs) and pursued the Paracelsian correspondence of macrocosm and microcosm. Visitors were taken down to see it; at the basement's other end lay cellars, pantries and the deep well. Tycho later added a second, smaller laboratory of five furnaces in the converted winter dining room (Thoren, Lord of Uraniborg, pp. 159, 224).
Fate. lost with Uraniborg; no trace of the furnaces survives

Stjerneborg — the star castle

reconstructedA1584 · Ven (Hven)site-stjerneborg
A separate, largely subterranean observatory built in 1584 just south of Uraniborg: five crypts beneath rotating cupolas, each giving one of the largest instruments a permanent, wind-sheltered mounting on solid ground. Stjerneborg ('star castle') answered the chief defect of Uraniborg's high galleries — that wind and an unstable footing spoiled the finest measurements. In his own words, Tycho built it “about the year 1584, on a hill outside the castle … with no small difficulty and expenditure a subterranean observatory with various cellars … of solid masonry,” his purpose “partly to have placed some of the most important instruments securely and firmly in order that they should not be exposed to the disturbing influence of the wind, and should be easier to use,” and partly to separate simultaneous observers so “they should not get in the way of each other” (Mechanica, trans. Ræder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, pp. 135–137).
Dimensions. outer premises 70 feet per side; the central semicircles 24 feet in diameter — Tycho's own figures (Mechanica 1946, p. 137; in his 259 mm foot ≈ 18 m and ≈ 6.2 m)
Fate. ruined after 1597; the crypts excavated and reconstructed in the 20th century — now the Tycho Brahe Museum

Warming room

The square central room; its flat cupola painted with Tycho's world-system and eight astronomers; alcoves O and Q for rest, table V for recording, clocks and an iron stove; its turf-covered vault above ground formed the Parnassus mound, bearing a one-alen brass Mercury turned by a mechanism (given in 1590 to Duke Heinrich Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel).

The printing house (Tycho's press)

lostA1584 · Ven (Hven)site-printing-house
Tycho's own printing house, established on Hven in 1584 so that he controlled his own means of publication and distribution. Its earliest known imprint is the memorial broadsheet Epitaphium Johannis Pratensis (1584); the earliest DATED piece is the occasional pøm Carmen ad Jacobum Ulfeldium, inscribed 'Uraniburgi, 7 Kal. Decemb.' = 25 November 1584 (Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, p. 176 — correcting the sometimes-cited 27 November 1584, which conflates the date and the piece). The first true book was Elias Olsen Morsing's Diarium astrologicum et meteorologicum / Calendarium (calendar set late 1585, issued 1586). The press went on to produce De mundi (1588), the Danish-language Flemløs Astrologia (1591), the Epistolae (1596) and the advance sheets of the Progymnasmata (1592) — a work only completed at Prague in 1602.
Fate. lost; the press and types dispersed after Tycho left Hven

The paper mill

lostB1589–1597 · Ven (Hven)site-paper-mill
The paper mill on Hven that fed Tycho's press — its production a recurring concern in the correspondence (the two papermakers who absconded delayed the Progymnasmata, as Tycho complained to Hájek). Royal chancery records fix the mill's economics and fate: a privilege of 2 March 1592 ordered all inhabitants of Nørrejylland to sell their old linen rags (Lumper) to Tycho before anyone else, since he 'har anlagt en Papirmølle paa Hveen' and needed them to make paper (KB 1588–92 p. 750). A demolition order of 26 June 1602 to the new lensmand Cort Barleben locates the works 'syd for Uraniborg' and calls it a 'Stampemølle eller Papirmølle,' by then wholly derelict, to be torn down and its usable timber and stone re-used (KB 1596–1602 p. 751). The mill dam was built by Valentin von Spangenberg (also written 'Valenthin'), a hydraulic engineer previously employed by Frederick II at Kronborg (1578–88), who arrived on Hven in 1589. The Meteorological Diary records on 26 June 1589 that Valentin promised to complete the mølledæmning (mill dam) within four weeks, and on 22 July 1590: 'Abijt Valentinus opere aggeris apud molendinum confecto' — Valentin departed after completing the dam work (Vellev 2017, from TBOO IX). Tycho named the paper mill's purpose explicitly in a letter to Christoph Rothmann of 24 November 1589 (TBOO VI); Christian IV ordered oak timber felled for the stamp press in a letter to Kirsten Lindenov (Steen Bille's widow, Tycho's aunt) dated 19 March 1590 (Kancelliets Brevbøger 1588–1592, 360). Its ruined site was rediscovered by the amateur astronomer N. A. Møller Nicolaisen (1874–1954), who on a 1929 visit to Hven noticed a man-made mound and identified it as the fallen paper mill; the Scandinavian Tycho Brahe Foundation funded his excavations of 1933–34, an archæological sensation of the period (Vellev 2002).
Fate. lost; derelict by 1602 and demolished for salvage on royal order (26 June 1602, to lensmand Cort Barleben; KB 1596–1602 p. 751); site rediscovered and excavated 1933–34

Bohemia — the exile 5 sites

The Belvedere (Royal Summer Palace) — Tycho's Prague Musaeum

extantB1599–1635 · Praguesite-belvedere
The Renaissance Royal Summer Palace (Belvedere) in the Royal Garden below Prague Castle. Tycho is reported to have made Prague observations 'in the arcades of the building' (Pierre Bergeron, 1607); after his death in 1601 the Belvedere became a memorial 'Astronomical Museum' housing the astronomy and exact-science part of Rudolf II's collections — the large instruments together with portraits of astronomers (Ptolemy, Albategnius, Copernicus, and two of Tycho himself) and of their royal patrons (Alfonso X, Charles V, Rudolf II, Frederik II of Denmark). The two surviving Tycho-associated sextants by Bürgi and Habermel passed through this collection on their way to the National Technical Museum. Dreyer (1890, p. 365) corroborates the connection from the other side: the Emperor agreed to buy Tycho's own Hven instruments from the family for 20,000 thaler; Tengnagel, as scientific heir from 1602, denied Kepler access to them and had them vaulted under Curtius' house, and Kepler later recorded the 'instrumenta Braheana' as standing 'in viridario Caesaris' (the Emperor's garden, i.e. this Belvedere) in October 1604 — before they were destroyed in the 1619 Bohemian rising against the Habsburgs. Not to be confused with Tycho's principal Prague-period working sites, Benátky nad Jizerou and the Curtius house — the latter the very building under which the instruments were stored. Grade B: the 'Musaeum' reading is Fučíková's, and Tycho's own use of the Belvedere is reported, not firmly documented.
Fate. the building survives; its astronomical contents dispersed after 1612 and removed to the Gallery Building by 1635

Benátky nad Jizerou — Tycho's first Bohemian observatory

extantB1599–1600 · Benátky nad Jizerousite-benatky
The hilltop castle at Benátky nad Jizerou, about 30 km north of Prague, granted to Tycho by Rudolf II in 1599 as his first Bohemian observatory. He was given leave to build wooden observing cubicles (now vanished); the portion available to him ran to three floors of nearly 500 m² each. Here Johannes Kepler joined Tycho in February 1600, before Tycho moved to Prague proper (Thoren, Appendix 5).
Fate. the hilltop castle survives (renovated, intended to house a small Tycho museum); the wooden observing cubicles are gone

The Curtius (Kurtz) house — Tycho's Prague residence and place of death

lostB1600–1601 · Praguesite-curtius-house
The summer home built by the imperial vice-chancellor Jacob Kurtz (Curtius), a few minutes' walk west of the Imperial Castle on the Hradčany hill — Tycho's principal Prague residence for most of his Bohemian years (the 20,000-gulden edifice he described) and the house in which he died on 24 October 1601. After his death the imperial-purchased instruments were vaulted under this very house before passing to the Belvedere garden (Dreyer, p. 365; cf. site-belvedere). Only a 7×16 m foundation remnant survives by a later school (Thoren, Appendix 5).
Fate. demolished; only a 7×16 m foundation remnant survives by a later school; statues of Tycho and Kepler stand on the site (since 1984)

The Schwarzenberg (Rožmberk) palace — Tycho's last banquet

extantC1601 · Praguesite-schwarzenberg
The Renaissance palace on Hradčany square, then owned by Petr Vok z Rožmberka (who had acquired it from Rudolf II by exchange in 1600) — by Thoren's reckoning (Appendix 5) the site of the banquet of 13 October 1601 at which Tycho fell fatally ill. The contemporary story holds that, out of deference to his host Petr Vok, he held his urine too long at table; he sickened with a bladder/uraemic ailment and died eleven days later, on 24 October 1601, at the Curtius house. Grade C: the banquet's location at the Rožmberk palace follows Thoren; the death-by-retention tale is contemporary tradition, not established fact (the 2010 exhumation only excluded mercury poisoning — see the Receptio record of the 2010 exhumation).
Fate. the palace survives on Hradčany square (now a museum)

Church of Our Lady before Týn — Tycho's grave

extantA1601 · Praguesite-tyn-church
The Church of Our Lady before Týn on Prague's Old Town Square, where Tycho was buried on 4 November 1601. His tomb is marked by a relief effigy in armour with one hand on a celestial globe. The grave's afterlife — the 1901 and 2010 exhumations and the long Danish–Czech contest of memory — is modelled in the Reception pillar.

7The journeys

Twenty-one documented route sequences. Only the stations the sources name are listed, in the order the evidence supports; the lines drawn on the map join those stations and are not claimed roads. Where the accounts differ — and for the flight from Denmark in 1597 three incompatible routes are on record — the disagreement is printed rather than resolved.

First study journey: Copenhagen to Leipzig, February–March 1562

A14 February 1562 – 24 March 1562journey-copenhagen-leipzig-1562
PurposeThe prescribed foreign educational journey of a young Danish noble: sent by Jørgen Brahe and Inger Oxe to Germany's best law school, nominally for jurisprudence, with the twenty-year-old Anders Sørensen Vedel as preceptor, guardian and treasurer.
Copenhagen → Wittenberg → Leipzig
Departed Copenhagen 14 February 1562, arrived Leipzig 24 March — five and a half weeks by ship across the southern Baltic, then on horseback along the Elbe and Saale, passing through Wittenberg and riding two more days to Leipzig. Wittenberg is the only intermediate station any source names; Dreyer, Friis, Norlind, Jönsson and Christianson 2020 name none. Kinsmen had arranged a good reception in Leipzig in advance.
Evidence (9)
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 16
“Vedel and his pupil left Copenhagen on the 14th February 1562, and arrived at Leipzig on the 24th March following”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871, p. 12
“De forlode Kjøbenhavn ... den 14. Februar 1562, og ankom til Leipzig den 24. Marts.”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 16
“till vilken han anlände d. 24 mars 1562 efter att ha lämnat Köpenhamn d. 14 febr.”
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), p. 14
“The journey by ship across the Baltic and on horseback along the roads that followed the Elbe and the Saale rivers took five weeks”
Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga (2006), p. 44
“I februari 1562 korsade de södra Östersjön, för att därefter färdas längs Elbe till Wittenberg, varifrån de landvägen fortsatte till Leipzig”
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), pp. 14–16
“Den 14 februari 1562 lämnade han Danmark i sällskap med den 20-årige Anders Sorensen Vedel.”
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 22
“in February 1562 they set off to Germany's best law school at Leipzig University”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 5
“destinatus cum Paedagogo Lipsiam, illac sub Martii finem pervenit”
Christianson, 'Tycho Brahe's Facts of Life' (1970), p. 24
“He left Copenhagen on February 14, 1562.”
The sources disagree. A source record spanning the whole decade of the 1560s, with an ordering its own source cannot verify after Leipzig, is reduced here to the attested Copenhagen–Leipzig leg.

Return from Leipzig to wartime Denmark, May–June 1565

A17 May 1565 – June 1565journey-leipzig-home-1565
Purposetravel-transit
Leipzig → Wittenberg → Rostock → Copenhagen → Helsingborg → Malmö → Knutstorp
The best-dated of the early journeys: Tycho and Vedel left Leipzig on 17 May 1565 (Hegelund's date), passed through Wittenberg, reached Rostock on 25 May (Stephanius), and crossed the war-time Baltic to Copenhagen without meeting hostile cruisers, the Danish and Swedish fleets massing in the Sound. The onward legs — Copenhagen, Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp, with latitude determinations under way — are Norlind's probable reading of the pole-height list in the oldest observation journal. Gassendi has a direct sail from Rostock to the fatherland.
Evidence (7)
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), pp. 19–20
“They passed through Wittenberg to see Schultz... reached Rostock on 25 May... Tycho proceeded to Helsingborg, Malmö, and finally Knudstrup Manor”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 21–22
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 18
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 20
“Annotationes interiectae occasione puto itineris Lipsia per Witebergam, Rostochium”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 8
Christianson, 'Tycho Brahe's Facts of Life' (1970), Christianson, Facts of Life (F&F 1970), p. 24
“He left Leipzig on May 17, 1565. He came to Rostock on May 25, 1565.”
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 29
“In late May 1565, after three years in Leipzig, Tycho and Vedel came home to a Denmark locked in war”
The sources disagree. Gassendi's reading of the return as a recall occasioned by Jørgen Brahe's death is rejected (Norlind): the uncle died 21 June, a month after departure. The Scanian waypoints rest on the journal inference; Gassendi has the ship sail 'recta in patriam' from Rostock. Christianson 2020 ends the journey at Aalborghus rather than Knutstorp (see stay-knutstorp-1565 disputes). A parallel stationless record of the same return (Jönsson: probably at Jørgen Brahe's urging; Christianson 2020: home in late May) was merged here.

Second departure: Denmark to Wittenberg, April 1566

Ato 15 April 1566 (arrival within the month)journey-second-study-tour-1566
Purposeeducation
Knutstorp → Wittenberg
Early in 1566 Tycho left Denmark for the second time — without a noble hovmester, in the company of the M.A. Hans Aalborg and at least one other Dane — arriving at Wittenberg on 15 April 1566 (Stephanius: 'Returned to Wittenberg on April 15, 1566, from his fatherland'). Gassendi frames the departure as hastened 'not without a show of anger' at his relations' contempt for his studies.

Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 21

Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 9
The sources disagree. Point of departure within Denmark unspecified by most sources; Christianson 2020 has Aalborghus, Thoren the family seat (Knudstrup).

Plague flight: Wittenberg to Rostock, September 1566

A16 September 1566 – 24 September 1566journey-plague-flight-1566
Purposetravel-transit
Wittenberg → Rostock
An epidemic emptied the congested little university town: Tycho and Aalborg left Wittenberg on 16 September 1566 and reached Rostock on 24 September, 'fleeing on account of the plague' (Stephanius), an eight-day journey; he matriculated at Rostock the following month.
Evidence (7)

“Den 16. September forlod han Wittenberg; den 24. i samme Maaned ankom han til Rostock”

“Leaving there September 16, he came to Rostock September 24, fleeing on account of the plague.”
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), p. 22

Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 21
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 30
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 9
The sources disagree. Departure 16 September (Stephanius, Dreyer, Friis, the Nationalmuseet essays) against Thoren's 14 September; arrival 24 September is agreed. Stephanius followed.

Purposebirth-family
Rostock → Denmark (unspecified)
In the summer of 1567 Tycho travelled home from Rostock to order his affairs and visit kinsmen and friends; dissatisfied with his reception, he set out again at the close of the year. No waypoints are named by any source.

Third trip abroad: Denmark to Rostock, New Year 1568

ADecember 1567 – 1 January 1568journey-return-rostock-1568
Purposeeducation
Denmark (unspecified) → Rostock
After his twenty-first birthday and the Christmas holidays at home, Tycho embarked on his third trip abroad, arriving at Rostock on 1 January 1568 — this time entirely without a tutor, amid friction with his father over the direction of his studies.
Evidence (5)
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 27–28

Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 32

Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 pp. 25–26

Southward across Germany: Rostock to Basel, 1568

Bto September 1568 (arrival within the year)journey-south-to-basel-1568
Purposeeducation
Rostock → Nuremberg → Basel
During 1568 — under the shadow of the unpaid duel fine, and freed from law by the canonry promise — Tycho travelled south across Germany, purchasing instruments at Nuremberg (Christianson 2020), and was matriculated at Basel by the autumn. The exact route is otherwise unrecorded: Thoren allows a possible meeting with his brother Steen at Arnstadt for the dubbing by Count Günther of Schwarzburg, and a 'perhaps Wittenberg' — both too hedged to log as stays. The traditional intermediate Wittenberg residence (Gassendi, Dreyer, Friis) is rejected by Norlind.

Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), pp. 30, 93
“During the summer of 1568, Tycho traveled southward across Germany. Perhaps he met his brother Steen at Arnstadt”
