Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 28–29
“he was at Wittenberg some time in 1568, and went to Basle in the course of the same year”
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 32, 34 hedged early legs; Nuremberg and Ingolstadt placed on this southbound route in this account
Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga (2006), Håkansson ed. 2006, scan p. 43
“Från Rostock reste han till Wittenberg, varifrån han snart fortsatte till Basel”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 11
“Anno postea partim illeic partim Wittebergae transacto, lustrare ulterius Germaniam decrevit”
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), p. 17
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 27 Friis has winter 1568–69 at Wittenberg and routes Rostock–Wittenberg–Augsburg with no Basel residence at all
The sources disagree. The intermediate 1568 Wittenberg stay (Gassendi 'partim illeic partim Wittebergae'; Dreyer with a Mechanica citation; Friis, who even winters him there 1568–69 and omits Basel entirely) is rejected by Norlind — Dreyer's citation is to the wrong edition's foliation, and the documented Basel matriculation supersedes Friis's route; the Zusammenfassung keeps only 'über Wittenberg (?)'. Thoren's Arnstadt/Castle Neideck meeting for Steen Brahe's dubbing is speculative in both Thoren and Christianson 2020 and is not logged as a stay.

Basel to Augsburg by the Danube road, early 1569

BDecember 1568 – 14 April 1569journey-basel-to-augsburg-1569
Purposeeducation
Basel → Freiburg im Breisgau → Lauingen → Ingolstadt → Augsburg
Leaving Basel at the turn of 1568/69, Tycho turned the road to Augsburg into a tour of south-German astronomical practitioners: Schreckenfuchs's planetary models at Freiburg, the night-long dinner with Leovitius at Lauingen, and (on Norlind's redating) the call on Philip Apian at Ingolstadt, reaching Augsburg in time to observe from 14 April 1569.
Evidence (6)
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), p. 30
“In Freiburg he noted some celestial models... In Lauingen he was invited home... In Ingolstadt he met Phillip Apian... Only in the spring of 1569 when he reached the old imperial city of Augsburg”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 23–24 Lauingen and Ingolstadt on the Basel–Augsburg leg, argued to spring 1569
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 28–30
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 34–36
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 pp. 27–28
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 11
The sources disagree. Waypoint order and attachment vary: Thoren has Freiburg–Lauingen–Ingolstadt after Basel; Christianson 2020 places Nuremberg and Ingolstadt before Basel and Freiburg as an excursion from it; Gassendi, Dreyer and Håkansson move the Ingolstadt call to the 1570 homeward journey. Norlind's spring-1569 placement of Ingolstadt is followed.

Homeward from Augsburg to Helsingborg, May–December 1570

A16 May 1570 – 30 December 1570journey-augsburg-home-1570
Purposebirth-family
Augsburg → Wittenberg → Rostock → Helsingborg
An unhurried homecoming whose route, previously unknown, is partly fixed by Norlind's find: last Quadrans Maximus observation at Augsburg 16 May 1570; the Textor album leaf proving Wittenberg on 9 September 1570; probably a call on the Rostock professors (Thoren); across the Baltic; and observing at Helsingborg Castle by 30 December 1570, the sextant and unfinished globe left in Paul Hainzel's keeping at Augsburg. The older tradition routed him through Ingolstadt with a Copenhagen landfall; the motive — his father's illness — is itself questioned.
Evidence (7)
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 26–28
“Witteberge: Anno: 1570: sept: 9.” last Augsburg observation 16 May 1570; Helsingborg observations 30 December 1570
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), p. 36
“Tycho did not reach Wittenberg until September and probably visited with his former professors in Rostock before crossing the Baltic to Denmark”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 34–35
“Tycho Brahe left Augsburg in 1570, but the exact month is not known, nor the route by which he travelled”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 30
“forlod idetmindste Augsburg henimod Slutningen af Aaret, og allerede inden Aarets Udgang var han i Helsingborg”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 16
“Traiecto Danubio, vidit Ingolstadii Philippum Appianum... postquam tamen Hafniam appulsus”
Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga (2006), Håkansson ed. 2006, p. 49
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 40
The sources disagree. Friis's late-1570 departure from Augsburg is superseded by the album leaf (Wittenberg 9 September). The Ingolstadt call placed on this journey by Gassendi, Dreyer and Håkansson is redated to spring 1569 by Norlind (followed). Gassendi's Copenhagen landfall, court salute and 1571 homecoming date are rejected on the 30 December 1570 Helsingborg observations (Norlind). The father's-illness motive (Friis, Jönsson, Håkansson 'probably') is doubted by Norlind given the unhurried pace and Otte's death only in May 1571. The Rostock call is Thoren's 'probably'.

The early-1574 Skane-Oresund observing circuit

CJanuary 1574 – May 1574journey-skane-oresund-circuit-1574
PurposeObservation circuit between the family estates, the Bille abbey and the capital, documented from Tycho's manuscript observation books by the 1746 Danske Magazin compiler.
Knutstorp → Herrevad Abbey → Copenhagen
The compiler's continuous itinerary sentence has Tycho at the start of 1574 on his Skåne estates, observing at Herrevad Abbey in March and April (Dreyer, from the same books, extends the run into May), and in Copenhagen from late April and May, where he mostly lived for the rest of the year. The compiler also places him on Hven on 22 February 1574 'af hvad Anledning vides ikke'; that leg is excluded here because Dreyer showed the observed Mars-moon conjunction fits 22 February 1576, not 1574 — the first documented Hven visit therefore falls outside this period.
Evidence (2)
Kancelliets Brevbøger vedr. Danmarks indre Forhold (Rigsarkivet, ed. Laursen), Danske Magazin II (1746), pp. c. 189–190
“Udi Begyndelsen af Aaret 1574. haver han opholdet sig paa sit Gods i Skaane, og i Februario ... har han været paa Hveen ... J Martio og April Maaneder har han observeret paa Herisvad Kloster, og sidst in Aprili saa vel som in Majo befindes han at have været i Kiobenhavn”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 73; p. 86 note
“In March, April, and May 1574 Tycho observed at Heridsvad” Dreyer's note refuting the 1574 Hven dating: moon and Mars fit 22 February 1576
The sources disagree. The compiler (after Langebek, Danske Magazin ii. 194) has Tycho on Hven with observations on 22 February 1574; Dreyer (p. 86 n.) refutes the dating — on that day the moon was a few days old and Mars on the other side of the heavens, whereas the observed close Mars-moon conjunction fits 22 February 1576 exactly. The Hven leg is excluded from the route; the first Hven visit belongs to 1576.

The grand tour of 1575

AMarch 1575 – December 1575journey-grand-tour-1575
PurposeDouble agenda: openly, Frederick II's commission to scout artists, artisans and technicians for the Kronborg project (reported at Sorø at Yuletide); privately, reconnaissance for a permanent foreign home — resolved secretly in favour of Basel.
Copenhagen → Kassel → Frankfurt am Main → Basel → Venice → Innsbruck → Augsburg → Regensburg → Nuremberg → Saalfeld → Wittenberg → Sorø Abbey → Knutstorp
Departing about March 1575 as a grand seigneur with servants, portable instruments and probably Flemløs, Tycho went first to Kassel (late March-April, eight to ten days with Wilhelm IV), then to the Frankfurt spring book fair, southwest to Basel (the emigration target chosen), over the Alps to Venice — his farthest south — and back over the Brenner via Innsbruck to Augsburg (late summer to late October: the cracked Schissler globe, Gemperlin recruited), downriver to Regensburg for Rudolf II's coronation on 1 November (Hagecius, the Commentariolus), then home via Nuremberg (Camerarius, Labenwolf), Saalfeld (Reinhold's manuscripts) and Wittenberg (Schuler's triquetrum, the crypto-Calvinist purge), reaching the Yuletide court at Soro by December and Knutstorp for the winter. The outward order Kassel-Frankfurt-Basel-Venice and the return order Augsburg-Regensburg-Nuremberg-Saalfeld-Wittenberg are the consensus of the ordered sources; the two fixed anchors are the spring fair and the 1 November coronation.
Evidence (10)
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 67–73 Kassel late March; Frankfurt fair, Basel, Alps, Venice; Augsburg late summer; Regensburg 1 Nov; Nuremberg and Saalfeld; Wittenberg and return; Soro report
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 78–84
“he went first to Cassel... From Cassel, Tycho went to Frankfurt-on-the-Main... thence to Basle... through Switzerland to Venice... in the first instance to Augsburg... At Ratisbon... From Ratisbon Tycho returned home via Saalfeld and Wittenberg”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 pp. 53–56
“Han begav sig først til Cassel ... Fra Cassel begav han sig til Frankfurt am Main ... Herfra drog han til Basel ... opholdt sig nogle Dage i Venedig ... Fra Venedig drog han til Augsburg ... Han begav sig nu til Regensburg”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), pp. 27–31
“Contendit porro primum in Hassiam... Francofurtum ad Maenum petiit... Basilea placuit... dies aliquot transegit Venetiis... Vindelicorum Augusta transiit... Ratisbonam cum pervenisset... Inter redeundum vidit Saltfeldiae... Vidit etiam Wittebergae”
Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga (2006), Håkansson ed. 2006, pp. 54–55
“Varen 1575 overgav han i varje fall katedern... I april anlande han till... Kassel... Darefter gick farden vidare mot Regensburg”
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), pp. 24, 111
“Första anhalten på denna rekognosceringsresa blev Kassel... Den 1 november 1575 var Tycho närvarande i Regensburg”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 16, 65-69 the journey characterised as reconnaissance for settling abroad; Kassel a week, Frankfurt fair, probably Innsbruck-Brenner-Trento-Treviso to Venice, return probably the same way, Augsburg, Regensburg, short Nuremberg stop, Saalfeld and Wittenberg hedged
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), pp. 93–100, 102 the full sequential itinerary; the court at Sorø Abbey for the Christmas season
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), scan pp. 15, 28
“Tycho Brahe traveled as a courtier, and his route went mainly to courtly centers of learning.”
Mosley, Bearing the Heavens (2007), Mosley 2007, pp. 40, 166
“a visit made in 1575, during the last of his youthful travels around Europe”
The sources disagree. Christianson 2000's station list (Kassel, Venice, Regensburg, Augsburg, Nuremberg, Basel) is an unordered narrative enumeration; the ordered sources (Dreyer, Friis, Gassendi, Christianson 2020, Jönsson, Håkansson, Thoren) agree on Kassel-Frankfurt-Basel-Venice-Augsburg-Regensburg. Gassendi, Dreyer, Friis and Jönsson omit Nuremberg on the return; Christianson 2020, Norlind and Thoren place it after Regensburg — included. Norlind leaves the Saalfeld and Wittenberg placements hedged; the consensus 1575-return placement is followed. Padua (Jönsson 'hogst troligt') and Trento/Treviso (Norlind probable route) are excluded from the canonical route. Departure date: Thoren c. March 1575; Dreyer 'shortly after' the lectures ended early in 1575; Jönsson 'at the beginning of 1575'.

The Ibstrup summons and Hven decision circuit, February 1576

A11 February 1576 – 22 February 1576journey-hven-decision-circuit-1576
Purposecourt-patronage
Knutstorp → Ibstrup → Knutstorp → Herrevad Abbey → Copenhagen → Frederiksborg → Ven (Hven)
A fully dated circuit, documented by Tycho's own account written three days after the audience, that converted the planned Basel emigration into the Hven enterprise: the pre-dawn royal courier at Knutstorp (11 February), the same-day ride to the private audience at Ibstrup, back to Knutstorp to deliberate, consultation rides to Herrevad (Steen Bille) and Copenhagen (Pratensis, Dançay), acceptance at Frederiksborg on 18 February with the 500-daler pension, and the first crossing to Hven with its first observation on 22 February 1576.
Evidence (4)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), scan p. 29–32
“He arrived at Ibstrup that same day... he renewed his service to King Frederick II... on 18 February 1576... Four days after his royal audience at Frederiksborg Castle, Tycho Brahe was on the island of Hven.”
Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga (2006), Håkansson ed. 2006, scan pp. 50–52
“En tidig morgon i februari 1576 kom en kunglig budbarare till Knutstorp... redan samma eftermiddag anlande han till det kungliga jaktgodset Ibstrup... red han en vecka senare till Frederiksborgs slott”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 84–85
“He started the same day, and arrived in the evening at the king's hunting-lodge at Ibstrup, near Copenhagen”
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), p. 27
“Tycho Brahe gav sig omedelbart i vag mot Sjalland och hann samma dag fram till jaktslottet Ibstrup, dar kungen befann sig.”
The sources disagree. Thoren places the Herrevad and Copenhagen consultation legs in January 1576, before the summons; Christianson's mid-February ordering is followed for the route. Four per-source journey records collapsed into this one canonical circuit.

Final removal from Hven to Copenhagen (February–April 1597)

AFebruary 1597 – 11 April 1597journey-hven-copenhagen-1597
Purposeexile
Ven (Hven) → Copenhagen
The rolling evacuation of the observatory: Tycho's letter to Rantzau of 22 February 1597 — overlooked by previous biographers (Thoren) — shows the move to Copenhagen already in progress; the last Hven observation was made 15 March; the first crossing over was 18 March, the day the pension stopped; movable instruments, library, laboratory and press were boated to the Farvergade complex through the spring; and on 11 April 1597 the diary records the household's entry into the 'novum Museum Hafniense'. He never returned to the island.
Evidence (6)
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), pp. 370–371
“left Hven for the last time, shortly after Easter, on the twenty-ninth of March”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 238 note rejects the observing-ledger's 'die 29 Aprilis': Easter 1597 fell 27 March; the household entered the new house 11 April; Tycho's own German account gives over two months at Copenhagen
Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen (1992), Christianson 2000, pp. 207–208; Björklund 1992, p. 97 (Bilag 4)
“tog i April Maaned ind i sit Huus udi Kiøbenhavn, hvorhen han lod sig føre de mindst betydelige af hans Instrumenter, og hele sit Trykkerie”
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), pp. 201–202
“Tycho Brahe and his familia moved into the new 'museum' in Copenhagen. He would never return to the island of Hven.”
Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen (1921), Nielsen bibliography layer §1.2
“On 29 April 1597 Tycho left Hveen forever, his press materiel and most of the instruments accompanying him via Copenhagen to Wandsbeck.”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 255
“Han bröt alltså upp från Hven i mars 1597”
The sources disagree. The final island departure: 29 March 1597 (Thoren; Dreyer's argument from Easter and the diary) vs the observing ledger's 'statim a Paschatis Festo die 29 Aprilis' repeated by Nielsen — 29 March followed (Dreyer's demonstration; Thoren concurs).

Out of Denmark: Copenhagen to Rostock (2 June – mid-June 1597)

B2 June 1597 (departure within the month)journey-copenhagen-rostock-1597
Purposeexile
Copenhagen → Køge → Vordingborg → Nykøbing Falster → Gedser → Rostock
On Thursday 2 June 1597 (Julian) Tycho, Kirsten, the six children, chaplain Wensøsil, students and servants — more than a score of people, with wagons bearing library, instruments, presses, the great globe and ironbound treasure chests, under armed escort — left Copenhagen and reached Rostock by mid-June. Christianson reconstructs the southern road through Køge and Vordingborg (his foster father's boyhood castles), the Falster crossing, Nykøbing, and embarkation at Gedser; the endpoints and dates are secure, the interior stations are reconstruction. The route deliberately retraced Tycho's boyhood geography, framed by the exempla of returned exiles Peter Oxe, Knud Brahe, Erik Sparre and Erik Lange.
Evidence (7)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), pp. 205, 208
“southward to Køge and on to Vordingborg... to Nykobing... to the port of Gedser... sailed to the free city of Rostock”
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), Christianson 2000, pp. 211, 213-214; Thoren 1990, p. 389; Björklund 1992, pp. 21, 47, 97 endpoints secure, interior stations Christianson's reconstruction
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 255
“Färden gick antagligen över Köge och Lübeck till Rostock.”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), scan pp. 206, 208
“Conduxit subinde onerariam navim... Vela igitur fecit Tycho aestate paene media, ac iter direxit Rostochium”
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), p. 127
“Den 2 juni 1597 steg Tycho Brahe och hans familj samt en del medlemmar av hans stab ombord på ett fartyg i Köpenhamn.”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 242 note
“He must, therefore, have left Copenhagen between the 1st and 10th June”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 235
“til Rostock, hvortil han ankom midt i Juni Maaned”
The sources disagree. Three incompatible route versions: (1) Christianson's overland caravan through Køge–Vordingborg–Falster–Nykøbing with the sea crossing from Gedser; (2) Norlind's 'probably over Køge and Lübeck to Rostock'; (3) a ship boarded at Copenhagen itself (Gassendi's hired cargo vessel; Jönsson; Friis 'fragtede et Skib'). The 2 June departure from Copenhagen is Tycho's own dated statement and secure; the mode and stations of the crossing are not — all three versions preserved. Gassendi's 'aestate paene media' (almost midsummer) is loose but compatible. Christianson 2000 calls 2 June a Saturday; 2 June 1597 (Julian) fell on a Thursday — the date itself, Tycho's own (Acta 124), is secure; the weekday is Christianson's slip.

Rostock to Wandsburg via Segeberg and Bramstedt (8 September – mid-October 1597)

A8 September 1597 – October 1597journey-rostock-wandsbek-1597
Purposeexile
Rostock → Doberan → Wismar → Segeberg → Bramstedt → Wandsbek
Fleeing the Rostock pestilence with no royal answer in hand, the familia left Rostock on 8 September 1597 and moved westward through Doberan (the Amt just pledged for Tycho's loan) and Wismar into Holstein, reaching the viceregal fortress of Segeberg by 17 September. Rantzau being at Bramstedt, Tycho wrote ahead stating his need of a residence near a printing city; at Bramstedt the viceroy received the party with open arms and lent Wandsburg over its lessee's head. The move formalised the friend-and-guest, not patron-client, relation with Rantzau. Settlement at Wandsbek followed in mid-October (Thoren, Dreyer, Friis) or late September (Christianson).
Evidence (6)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), pp. 211, 214
“took their leave of Rostock on 8 September 1597 and proceeded westward through Doberan and Wismar... By 17 September, they had arrived at Segeberg Fortress”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), Christianson 2000, pp. 217–220; Dreyer 1890, p. 266; Björklund 1992, p. 98 (Bilag 4) arrival late September (Christianson) or mid-October (Dreyer)
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 257, 260
“Färden gick sannolikt över Wismar till Segeberg i Holstein”
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), pp. 380–381
“Around the middle of October, therefore, Tycho settled into a nicely renovated old castle on the outskirts of Hamburg”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), scan p. 350 (index)
“Invitatus ab Henrico Rantzovio omnia Wandesburgum, per Hamburgum transfert” the goods moved via Hamburg; not a bodily Hamburg stay
Tycho Brahes Verden (Nationalmuseet, 2006), Håkansson ed. 2006, scan pp. 70–71; Tycho Brahes Verden, scan p. 214 early-September departure under armed escort (Håkansson) vs the Wandsbeck move 'from mid-October' (Bøggild-Johannsen)
The sources disagree. Wandsbek settlement: late September 1597 (Christianson) vs mid-October (Dreyer, Thoren, Friis, Björklund, Bøggild-Johannsen) — mid-October adopted, with Thoren's 8 October Bramstedt letter as the hinge. Thoren's unnamed 'first estate, too remote' is identified with Segeberg (same 17 September letter). Dreyer and Friis, lacking the Holstein stations, run Rostock direct to Wandsbek in mid-October — compression, not conflict, once the September stations are admitted.

The interrupted Prague journey: Wandsburg to Wittenberg via Harburg, Magdeburg and Dresden (29 September – 4 December 1598)

A29 September 1598 – 4 December 1598journey-wandsbek-wittenberg-1598
Purposecourt-patronage
Wandsbek → Harburg → Magdeburg → Wittenberg → Dresden → Wittenberg
The first push toward Rudolf II, doubling as a patronage campaign — each halt yielded a recommendation, deposition or princely contact. Out of Wandsburg just after Michaelmas, 29 September 1598, in a caravan of three or more coaches: the Harburg call on Duke Otto II (Mechanica inscribed 5 October); about eight days at Magdeburg (Rollenhagen; Erik Lange's notarised Ursus deposition; instruments stored; Kirsten and the daughters sent back to Wandsburg with Longomontanus); up the Elbe through Wittenberg (album leaf 25 October, the Jessenius acquaintance made in passing); a month at Dresden awaiting imperial instructions (Venice and Magini letters 28 November); then, advised to defer Prague for the plague, the hundred-kilometre retreat to Wittenberg, reached 4 December 1598, for the winter.
Evidence (9)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), scan pp. 233–235, 302
“Just after Michaelmas... 29 September 1598... The caravan progressed as far as Magdeburg, where they stayed for a week... to Dresden, where they remained for a month.”
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 188
“Around Michaelmas of 1598, Tycho and his familia departed Wandsburg Castle in a caravan of at least four coaches surrounded by retainers”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 (exact page in the bundled consultation)

Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 297–298; p. 406
“Till Böhmen och Prag bröt man upp först strax efter Michaeli, närmare bestämt i början på oktober.” Tycho's own brief descriptions in letters of December 1598 to Krag, Rosenkrantz, later Vedel
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), pp. 403–405
“For the first leg of the journey they traveled some two hundred kilometers to Magdeburg... he had retreated one hundred kilometers back to Wittenberg” the Magdeburg–Dresden passage ran through Wittenberg
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 263
“Kort efter reiste Tyge Brahe fra Wandesborg ... Men da han kom til Dresden” compressed route Wandsbek–Dresden–Wittenberg, without Harburg or Magdeburg
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 157
“non Pragam usque perrexerit, sed Wittebergae constiterit” maximally compressed: Wandsbek to Wittenberg
The album-amicorum leaves, in the Graphonomicon, Graphonomicon, specimens rundetaarn-boetius-album-wandsbek-1598, leaf-wittenberg-1598–10-25 and uppsala-waller-dk-00231 the album-leaf itinerary: Wandsbek 13 Sept; Wittenberg 25 Oct; Dresden 10 Nov
The Epistolarium's letters spine (Tychoniana), the Epistolarium's letters spine; the specimens as cited Wandsbek → Wittenberg [1598]; the 'Dresden excursion' framing rejected in favour of the biographies' sequence
The sources disagree. Departure: 29 September 1598 (Christianson) vs beginning of October (Norlind, Björklund Bilag 4). Route order: an earlier reading framed Wittenberg as reached c. 21 October with Dresden a mid-November excursion; the biographies' Magdeburg → Dresden (month) → Wittenberg 4 December is followed, the 25 October Wittenberg leaf explained by Thoren's note that the Elbe road passed through Wittenberg. Friis and Gassendi compress the route (omitting Harburg and Magdeburg, and Dresden in Gassendi's case). The press materiel and heavy instruments travelled separately and wintered at Magdeburg, reaching Prague only in 1600 (Christianson, p. 337; Nielsen; Wolfschmidt: November 1600).

Wittenberg to Prague via Pretzsch and Dresden, 14 June – early July 1599

A14 June 1599 – July 1599journey-wittenberg-prague-1599
Purposecourt-patronage
Wittenberg → Pretzsch → Dresden → Prague
The definitive move to imperial service on Coraduz's summons. The whole familia left Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 — the departure self-dated in Tycho's farewell album leaf, 'quo Witebergā discessi' — spent the first night at Castle Pretzsch with Johann Löser, and reached Dresden on 16 June, where the female household was left with Johann Tauchmann. Tycho crossed the Ore Mountains with his sons and Claus Mule in his finest carriage, Ursus fleeing Prague at his approach; arrival fell in late June or the first days of July, and the von Wicken album entry of 13 July 1599 attests him at Prague within the month. The family followed from Dresden after the first audience.
Evidence (7)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), p. 232
“Tycho Brahe and all his familia took leave of Wittenberg on 14 June 1599... He proceeded on to Prague in his finest carriage with his son, Tycho Tygesen, and a few servants.”
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 191, 196
Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen (1992), Christianson 2000, p. 238; Björklund 1992, pp. 98–99 (Bilag 4)
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), p. 410
“They left right after summer solstice, traveling en masse to Dresden... On arriving there 'about the beginning of July'”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 300; Zusammenfassung p. 438
“Den 14 juni 1599 g.st. bröt Tycho upp från Wittenberg till Prag”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 265
“Tyge Brahe begav sig nu paa Reisen dertil strax efter Paaske 1599, og han lagde Veien over Dresden”
The Epistolarium's letters spine (Tychoniana), Graphonomicon, specimens leaf-wittenberg-1599–06-14 and stralsund-khm-a-1993-160-wicken; the Epistolarium's letters spine
“Wittenberg → Prague [1599]. Entered the service of Rudolf II.”
The sources disagree. Friis dates the departure 'straight after Easter 1599' against the self-dated 14 June album leaf and all modern accounts — June followed. Departure style: Norlind and Thoren mark 14 June as old style; Christianson gives it without style. Arrival: late June (Christianson) vs 'about the beginning of July' (Thoren, from Tycho's own letter) — not resolvable below a fortnight.

The castle-inspection circuit: Lysá, Brandeis, Benátky (summer 1599)

BJuly 1599 – August 1599journey-castle-circuit-1599
Purposeproperty-administration
Prague → Lysá nad Labem → Brandýs nad Labem → Benátky nad Jizerou
Offered the choice of three imperial castles outside Prague 'zur Exercirung seines Studii' — each under a day or half-day from the city — Tycho was conducted around to see them all: Lysá, Brandeis and Benátky. Brandeis, sitting low and the Emperor's favourite hunting-lodge, and Lysá were passed over; Benátky was chosen for its raised site and open horizon. The order of the circuit is not given by any source; the route order here is the sources' listing order, not an itinerary.
Evidence (3)
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 273
“efter at han var bleven foert omkring til dem alle for at besee dem, valgte han det sidstnaevnte”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 281
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), p. 163
“quarum illi Caesar extra urbem optionem dedit, quasque sub Maij finem invisit, tres fuere... Brandisium... Lyssa... Benachia”
The sources disagree. Gassendi dates the circuit 'sub Maij finem' 1599 — irreconcilable with the late-June Prague arrival; the circuit is placed between the July audience and the 20–21 August removal.

Removal from Prague to Benátky via Brandeis, 20-21 August 1599

A20 August 1599 – 21 August 1599journey-prague-benatky-1599
Purposeproperty-administration
Prague → Brandýs nad Labem → Benátky nad Jizerou
The removal to the chosen castle. On the way from Prague Tycho datelined a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock from Brandeis, 20 August 1599 (new style), reporting a level six-hour road and that a captain of Brandeis would carry him and all his effects to Benátky the same or the following day; by 28 August his first instrument stood at Benátky. Christianson has him formally escorted there in late August.
Evidence (4)
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 273
“skrev han den 20. August (ny Stiil) fra Brandeis”
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 282
“On the way to Benatky, Tycho sent from Brandeis a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock, dated the 20th August”

Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), pp. 414–415
“By 28 August Tycho had his first instrument set up at Benatky”

Plague flight to Girsitz and back, November 1599 – January 1600

BNovember 1599 – January 1600journey-benatky-girsitz-1599
Purposetravel-transit
Benátky nad Jizerou → Girsitz (Jičice?) → Benátky nad Jizerou
Escape from the plague that killed two thousand in the Benátky district: in the first half of November 1599 Tycho moved the household to the castle or village of Girsitz (first letter 16 November) and returned to Benátky in the new year after six or seven weeks, the return date blurred by letters diplomatically addressed from Benátky.
Evidence (4)
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), p. 419
“to take the family thirty kilometers down river, to a castle called Girsitz, to escape the plague”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 302–306
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 283
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 196
The sources disagree. Direction and distance of Girsitz from Benátky differ across the sources (thirty kilometres downriver vs a few miles south vs 'near Kostelec') — see stay-girsitz-1599.

Final removal from Benátky to Prague, June 1600

AJune 1600 – August 1600journey-benatky-prague-1600
Purposecourt-patronage
Benátky nad Jizerou → Prague
The end of the Benátky observatory project. Rudolf II returned from Pilsen on 10 June 1600 and summoned his astronomer to the capital for constant consultation — a move Tycho's own 26 September 1600 letter calls made by imperial order ('beschehenes Anordnenn von dannen hieher nach Prage'), and which proved sudden and permanent. The Benátky observation series breaks off at the end of June 1600; the household passed through the Golden Griffin and the Hoffmann-neighbourhood house before the Curtius house; the instruments followed from Benátky, and the great ones from Hven via the Magdeburg transit dispute, to the Belvedere by October-November 1600. Only Tycho's effects, not Tycho, passed through Magdeburg.
Evidence (6)
Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990), p. 442
“On 10 June, however, the emperor returned home from Pilsen and summoned Tycho to Prague... he was asked to move to Prague, suddenly, and, as it turned out, permanently”
Friis, Breve og Aktstykker (1875), Friis 1871, p. 292; Friis 1875, doc. 43 (26 September 1600)
“beschehenes Anordnenn von dannen hieher nach Prage”
Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55), pp. 175, 216
“Tycho pertaesus incommodorum Benaticae, commorari amplius ea in arce non sustineret”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 306–307
Studnička, Prager Tychoniana (1901), Studnicka 1901, scan p. 67; Crossroads 2002, scan pp. 129–130
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 202
The sources disagree. Timing of the move: June 1600 (Thoren, Christianson, Studnicka's end-June observation break) vs beginning of July (Norlind) vs c. August (Dreyer); Friis's datelines bracket it 15 May – 26 September 1600. June followed.

8Chronology

Fifty-five years in one view. One lane per place, grouped by region; a bar for each documented stay, coloured by life-era. Solid bars are day- or month-dated; faded bars are approximate. The anchors — Leipzig, the long Hven residence, Benátky, Prague — carry the short visits that interleave them. Beneath the chart, the same evidence as a year-by-year index: for any year between 1546 and 1601, where he is documented to have been.

9The phantom register

Forty-three claims of presence that the evidence does not support: fiefs administered by letter, an estate declined, remote purchases long mistaken for visits, invitations that prove nothing about attendance, and legends the sources refute. Each entry states the circulating claim, gives the verdict — never visited, declined, disputed, debunked — and prints the evidence. Several are not places at all but classes of claim, which is why they are counted as presence claims and not as phantom places.

Debunked 12 claims

Carolinum tower, Prague (eclipse of 22 July 1599)

debunkedAnv-carolinum-tower-eclipse
The claim. Tycho observed the solar eclipse of 22 July 1599 from the tower of the old Collegium (Carolinum).
Tycho's own letter (TBOO VIII, 183) says the eclipse was observed at the Carolinum tower 'per Iohannem meum Hamburgensem, adstantibus aliis' — by his Hamburg assistant Johannes (Eriksen), with bystanders — while Tycho himself worked with quadrant and sextant at his residence. Christianson agrees: he 'sent Johannes Eriksen up the tower'. The Carolinum therefore never enters Tycho's personal itinerary on this evidence.
Evidence (2)
Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (2002), Crossroads 2002, p. 244
“Pragae quoque in turricula veteris Collegii ... per Iohannem meum Hamburgensem, adstantibus aliis”
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 195 Sent Eriksen up the tower; observed at his residence himself.

Copenhagen (Diet/herredag of 1597)

debunkedAnv-herredag-1597
The claim. Tycho attended (or could have attended) a Diet in 1597 over the Gellius case.
No Diet met in 1597: the Gellius Sascerides matrimonial case was assigned on 5 April 1597 to a special court under Peter Munk precisely 'because the Diet did not meet in 1597'. Any narrative that stages Tycho before a 1597 herredag is structurally impossible on the documented judicial arrangements of that spring.
Evidence (1)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), p. 202
“because the Diet did not meet in 1597”

Copenhagen (astronomical observations from the rampart)

debunkedBnv-copenhagen-observations
The claim. Tycho observed astronomically at Copenhagen during his visits from Hven, e.g. from the rampart tower by his Farvergade house.
Dreyer states flatly that 'No observations were made at Copenhagen': the lent bastion tower was intended for a planned astronomical building for practising residents, never used so by Tycho before 1597. The companion persecution story — that the town bailiff forbade him to observe from it in 1597 — rests solely on Tycho's own German justification and 'sounds very apocryphal' (Norlind). Copenhagen remains a grade-A place for residence and business, not for observation.
Evidence (2)
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 201, p. 239
“No observations were made at Copenhagen”
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 255 The 1597 prohibition story judged apocryphal.

Doberan (loan delivery)

debunkedBnv-doberan-loan
The claim. Tycho travelled to Doberan in 1597 to deliver the 10,000-daler loan to the Mecklenburg dukes.
Tycho only promised to bring the money to Doberan himself once the bond was corrected (September 1597); Friis records no execution of the promise. At the repayment end in 1601 it was Eske Bille and his servant who went to Doberan and Rostock — Tycho, then in Prague, was never there for the transaction. A probable simple road-stop at Doberan in September 1597 (Norlind) survives as a waypoint stay, distinct from this loan-delivery journey.
Evidence (1)
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 242; pp. 293–294 Promise only; Eske Bille executed the 1601 repayment errand.

Frankfurt book fairs (1579–98 attendance)

debunkedAnv-frankfurt-fairs
The claim. Tycho attended the Frankfurt book fairs in person as buyer and distributor.
From Hven, Tycho worked the fairs entirely at arm's length: marked-up fair catalogues sent via Vedel to a Copenhagen intermediary (May 1579), merchant-couriers and Copenhagen dealers; type fonts were obtained at the fair through agents, and Hans Aalborg distributed the Uraniborg broadsides at the 1585 fair. No source places Tycho at a fair. Distinct from the 1575 pass-through visit to Frankfurt, which is attested and kept as a stay.
Evidence (2)
Mosley, Bearing the Heavens (2007), Mosley 2007, p. 167 Purchases THROUGH the fairs only; no bodily attendance.
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 123, 136 Agents went: printer Joachim (1584), Hans Aalborg (1585).

Frauenburg (Frombork) / Danzig / Königsberg

debunkedAnv-frauenburg-1584
The claim. Tycho travelled to Frauenburg, Danzig and Königsberg in 1584 to verify Copernicus's latitude.
The 1584 Baltic expedition was made by the assistant Elias Olsen Morsing, sailing with the returning Danish embassy: Copenhagen 1 May, Frauenburg from 13 May, Königsberg 8–28 June, back on Hven 23 July, bringing Copernicus's triquetrum as Hannow's gift. Tycho stayed on Hven and celebrated the relic with a Latin poem. Four independent sources make the correction; readings of Friis's itinerary as Tycho's own travel are explicit errors.
Evidence (4)
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 125–126 Morsing's expedition, itinerary and triquetrum.
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 124–125 Morsing travelled; Tycho stayed home.
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 pp. 132–133
“lod ... en af sine Disciple, nemlig Elias Olai Cimber eller Morsing”
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), p. 50 Expedition carried out by Morsing, sent by Tycho.

Hven (Valkendorf in the prince's suite, 3 July 1592)

debunkedBnv-valkendorf-hven-1592
The claim. Christopher Valkendorf attended Prince Christian's visit to Hven on 3 July 1592, where the famous dog-kicking quarrel with Tycho occurred.
Dreyer is categorical: 'it is quite certain that Valkendorf did not attend the Prince on his visit to Hveen', and the dog-quarrel traditions in both the 1592 and the Huet versions rest 'on rumour only'. Friis had already judged the Valkendorf identification 'perhaps right, though by no means certain' and the enmity-origin accounts 'highly unreliable'. The visit of the prince stands; the quarrel scene does not.

Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), pp. 216–217, 233-234
“it is quite certain that Valkendorf did not attend the Prince”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 202
“hoist upaalidelige”

Kassel (return visits)

debunkedAnv-kassel-after-1575
The claim. Tycho returned to Kassel after his Easter 1575 visit, e.g. in 1586 or 1590.
The great Hven-Kassel collaboration ran entirely by correspondence and emissaries: Flemløse carried the letter of 1 March 1586 and reported on the Landgrave's improved instruments; Gellius Sascerides delivered De mundi in 1588. Tycho and Wilhelm IV never met again after April 1575. The Meteorological Diary's 'Kassel' field of 1 August 1590 is Rothmann's provenance — the Landgrave's mathematician arriving with Tycho — not a Tycho destination.
Evidence (4)
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 118, pp. 135–137 1586 errand was Flemløse's; the pair never met again after April 1575.
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 143, 145, 160 Collaboration by correspondence and emissaries.
The album-amicorum leaves, in the Graphonomicon, Brahe hand profile §5.4 Gellius carried De mundi to Kassel, 1588.
The Meteorological Diary 1582–1597 (via the Tychoniana Diarium), Diarium @1590–08-01
“Rediit Tycho vesperi cum Rothmanno, Landtgravii Mathematico”

Leipzig (second journey, November 1565)

debunkedAnv-leipzig-1565-second
The claim. Tycho made a second journey to Leipzig in November 1565 (so Dreyer, from a note in the observation journal).
Norlind rejects it outright: the journal note is a copyist's misreading of Tycho's own words in the 1573 nova tract ('Lipsiae tunc temporis studiorum gratia commorati' — recalling the 1562–65 residence), and 'a second journey to Leipzig can naturally not be spoken of'. The related recall-motive story — that the death of his uncle Jørgen called him home — also fails: the uncle died 21 June 1565, a month after Tycho had left Leipzig on 17 May.
Evidence (1)
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 20; pp. 20–21
“En andra resa till Leipzig kan det naturligtvis ej vara tal om”

Magdeburg (1599–1600 presence)

debunkedBnv-magdeburg-1599-1600
The claim. Tycho was at Magdeburg in the winter of 1599–1600 and/or during the 1600 instrument transport.
Only Tycho's materiel was at Magdeburg in those years: the press equipment sent ahead from Wittenberg, and the great instruments in transit from Ven to Prague, whose Magdeburg transit licence was eased with bribes of Bohemian wine. Likewise the autumn-1598 escort of his wife and daughters to Magdeburg was a companion's journey, Tycho being at Wittenberg. His one attested bodily presence at Magdeburg is October 1598, when the household's travel plan changed there — kept as a stay.
Evidence (3)
Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen (1921), Nielsen bibliography layer §1.4 Only press materiel there in winter 1599–1600.
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), p. 133 1600 transport: instruments and wine bribes, not Tycho.
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 264 The 1598 Magdeburg escort was a companion's; Tycho at Wittenberg.

Venice (late-career patronage)

debunkedBnv-venice-late-career
The claim. Tycho travelled to, or relocated to, Venice in connection with the Republic's patronage in his late career.
Pigatto's study calls the entire Venetian engagement 'a Failed Project': Tycho's Italian contacts ran through emissaries only — Gellius Sascerides at Padua 1589–93 and Franz Tengnagel, sent November 1598 with the Grimani presentation copy. No bodily presence of Tycho in Venice belongs to the Bohemian period. Distinct from the attested 1575 visit, which stands as a place-stay.
Evidence (1)
Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (2002), Crossroads 2002, scan pp. 187–189, 313 Emissaries only; 'a Failed Project'.

Villands Herred / Hammer ('the other Tyge Brahe')

debunkedAnv-tyge-jensen-brahe
The claim. Chancery entries on 'Tyge Brahe' of Villands Herred / 'til Hammer' are itinerary data for the astronomer.
They concern Tyge Jensen Brahe, a same-named kinsman: lensmand of Villands Herred (fief letter 1 March 1576) and of Hammer, stabbed to death by Eiler Krause on 6 August 1581. The Krause safe-conduct and reconciliation letters (1582–94), the Villands arrears, the 1580 funeral-procession summons and the 1587 guardianship entry all belong to the kinsman's family. The volume registers separate 'Tyge Jensen' from 'Tyge Ottesen, Lensmand p. Hveen' page by page — an identity guard for every user of this edition.
Evidence (1)
Kancelliets Brevbøger vedr. Danmarks indre Forhold (Rigsarkivet, ed. Laursen), Kancelliets Brevbøger 1576–79, pp. 17, 716–816 passim; 1580–83, pp. 11–771 passim; 1584–88, pp. 124, 126, 573, 745; 1588–92, pp. 126, 640, 679, 765; 1593–96, p. 238; 1596–1602, p. 35 Registers disambiguate the two men explicitly.

Never visited 14 claims

Alexandria, Egypt (affiliate observatory)

never visitedAnv-alexandria
The claim. Tycho established, or travelled to, the planned affiliate observatory at Alexandria.
The Egyptian station was a recurrent scheme only: proposed to the Doge of Venice in the letter of 28 November 1598, revived around 1600 with Tycho Tygesen and Claus Mule as intended staff, and never executed. The Mechanica's claim that the Venetian Senate approved 300 ducati for the project is unverified — no document has been found in the Venetian archives (Favaro and Norlind both searched). No travel by Tycho, or by anyone, took place.
Evidence (2)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), scan pp. 235, 331 Scheme proposed 1598, revived c.1600, never executed.
Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (2002), Crossroads 2002, scan pp. 187–189 Venetian funding claim unverified in the archives.

Breslau/Wrocław (Wittich library)

never visitedAnv-breslau-wittich-library
The claim. Tycho travelled to Breslau/Wrocław to collect Paul Wittich's library.
Tycho pursued the Wittich books for years by negotiation with the heirs, and the purchase was consummated remotely: Jacob Monaw brought the annotated De revolutionibus copies from Wrocław to Tycho in Prague in October 1600 — only two of Wittich's four annotated copies ever reached him. Tycho did not go to Silesia.
Evidence (2)
Gingerich & Westman, The Wittich Connection (1988) / Gingerich, Annotated Census (2002), Gingerich census extract §4 Copies brought TO Tycho in Prague by Monaw, October 1600.
The edition's register of refuted claims (unpublished), BRAHE — De revolutionibus (Prague NK 14 B 16) entry Monaw acquisition channel independently documented.

Copenhagen (Christian IV's wedding, November 1597)

never visitedBnv-wedding-1597
The claim. Tycho attended Christian IV's wedding to Anne Catherine of Brandenburg.
Tycho was in exile at Wandsburg. Viceroy Rantzau planned to attend, while Tycho sent him travel-health advice and instructions on what to answer if his return to Denmark were raised at court. He met the bride's parents only afterwards, at Bramstedt on 22 December 1597, as the Brandenburg delegation travelled home. His having never again set foot on Danish soil after 2 June 1597 (see the phantom register) independently excludes attendance.
Evidence (1)
Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen (1992), Christianson 2000, p. 226 In exile; met the bride's parents at Bramstedt afterwards.

Family rites off Hven (weddings, funerals, burials)

never visitedBnv-family-rites-absences
The claim. Tycho left Hven for family rites — Axel Brahe's second wedding, his brother-in-law's funeral, the burials of his children at Helsingborg (1576) and Väsby (1577), the Kågeröd mausoleum epitaph.
Ellefsen states the opposite of the natural assumption: at Axel's second wedding both Tycho and Sophie stayed on Hven, and when their sister Margrethe's husband died, Tycho did not leave Uraniborg; Inger Oxe's death and funeral he does not even mention. Verden records the children's burials and Tycho's authorship of the Helsingborg epitaph text without any attendance, and expressly doubts his personal involvement in the Kågeröd mausoleum epitaph. The pattern: Tycho wrote epitaphs from his island; he did not travel to graves.
Evidence (2)
Ellefsen, Søsteren og astronomen (2023), Ellefsen 2023, p. 154 Stayed on Hven for Axel's wedding; did not leave for the funeral.
Tycho Brahes Verden (Nationalmuseet, 2006), Tycho Brahes Verden, scan pp. 55, 219
“har han naeppe selv vaeret personligt involveret i”

Güstrow (Duke Ulrich's court)

never visitedBnv-guestrow
The claim. Tycho travelled to Güstrow to Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg's court in 1597.
The loan negotiation with the Mecklenburg dukes and the duke's intercession with Christian IV were conducted entirely in writing: at the end of July 1597 Tycho wrote from Rostock to Duke Ulrich, whose court was at Güstrow, and received a cordial reply within days. No source consulted records a bodily visit; the phantom arises from compressing the correspondence into a journey.
Evidence (1)
Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen (1992), Christianson 2000 pp. 216–217 Letters only; no visit recorded.

Hven (return after 1597)

never visitedAnv-hven-after-1597
The claim. Tycho returned to Hven (or to Danish soil) after leaving in 1597.
After the household moved to the Farvergade house on 11 April 1597 and embarked at Copenhagen on 2 June, Tycho never set foot on Hven or Danish soil again. The island was run by his bailiff David Pedersen; his sons and Claus Mule retrieved the remaining instruments in 1599–1600, and royal commissions were the only official visitors. Christianson and Jönsson both state the denial in categorical terms.
Evidence (3)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), scan pp. 208, 331
“He would never return to the island of Hven.”
Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen (1992), Christianson 2000 pp. 208, 211, 213; Björklund 1992 p. 32 Bailiff ran the island; commissions visited.
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), pp. 123, 127, 132
“Tycho Brahe skulle aldrig mer sätta sin fot på dansk jord”

Louvain (Arsenius/Mercator workshops)

never visitedBnv-louvain-arsenius-cross-staff
The claim. Tycho visited Louvain to acquire his Arsenius cross-staff.
The 1560s cross-staff was a product of the Louvain instrument-making tradition of Gemma Frisius, Mercator and Walter Arsenius, and the workshop pedigree has been read as a visit. Mosley treats Louvain only as the origin of that tradition — whose masters had in any case relocated (Mercator to Duisburg in 1551) — and no source places Tycho in Louvain; the acquisition was a remote purchase.
Evidence (1)
Mosley, Bearing the Heavens (2007), Mosley 2007, pp. 214–215 Louvain named only as tradition of origin; acquisition remote.

Nordfjord (Norwegian fief)

never visitedAnv-nordfjord
The claim. Tycho visited his Norwegian fief of Nordfjord.
Nordfjord was a pure revenue holding across its whole tenure (1578–96), administered through a bailiff whom Tycho once dismissed and imprisoned; the latitude work in Norway was Flemløse's. Christianson states the denial outright — 'this Norwegian fief, which Tycho never visited'. The chancery record shows the len only at its end: recalled 16 March 1586 and compensated with 400 daler yearly from the Helsingør toll. No source claims a journey.
Evidence (4)

“this Norwegian fief, which Tycho never visited but administered through a bailiff”
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 162, 170 No visit recorded 1578–96; agents (bailiff, Flemløse) did the work.

Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 242–250 Fief treated purely as revenue administration; no bodily presence asserted.

Pilsen (imperial court in plague exile)

never visitedAnv-pilsen
The claim. Tycho followed Rudolf II to Pilsen during the 1599–1600 plague displacement of the court.
When plague drove the court from Prague in September 1599, the emperor went to Pilsen; Tycho stayed at Benátky (and the Girsitz refuge), sending Rudolf the formula for his Paracelsian plague medicament and communicating exclusively through the courier Daniel Fels, documented 6 January – 7 May 1600. In June 1600 Tycho was still writing that the emperor remained at Pilsen. Norlind's index entry 'Pilsen' concerns the court, not a Tycho stay.
Evidence (3)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), pp. 277, 302 Courier Daniel Fels the only channel; no visit.
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 196 Tycho stayed at Benátky, sent the plague remedy.
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 305–306 Index 'Pilsen' = the court's stay, not Tycho's.

Presentation-copy destinations (Oxford, Paris, Florence, Vienna, Gotha...)

never visitedBnv-presentation-destinations
The claim. The destinations of Tycho's presentation copies (Bodleian/Oxford, Paris, Venice, Florence, Vienna, Gotha etc.) imply his presence there.
The Mechanica / De revolutionibus-era presentation network was serviced entirely by couriers and intermediaries: Wotton took the Grimani copy to England, Tengnagel carried the Magini copy and the 1600 Grimani mission, Sascerides and Monaw served other routes. No dedication despatch in the Mosley appendix attests Tycho at any destination. A standing guard against reading the gift network as an itinerary — the books travelled; the astronomer did not.
Evidence (1)
Mosley, Bearing the Heavens (2007), Mosley 2007, Appendix I; Graphonomicon, specimen bodleian-mechanica-grimani Courier network fully documented; no presence claims.

Sweden proper (within its 16th-century borders)

never visitedBnv-sweden-proper
The claim. Tycho visited Sweden.
A standing trap of anachronism: Ven and Scania, where Tycho was born, lived and held his fief, only became Swedish in 1658/1660. Within Sweden's borders as they stood in his lifetime, Jönsson states flatly that the Scanian nobleman 'never set his foot on Swedish soil'. Any claimed stay in 16th-century Sweden proper contradicts the source base; the many 'Sweden' locations in this gazetteer are modern-country labels for then-Danish Scania.
Evidence (1)
Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025), p. 7
“never set his foot on Swedish soil during his lifetime”

Ven (visit by Frederick II)

never visitedBnv-frederik2-ven
The claim. Frederick II, Tycho's great patron, visited Hven.
A reverse-visit phantom worth registering against the island's glittering guest list: 'remarkably, the star-researcher's great patron, Frederik II' was never among the visitors to Ven, though Queen Sophie, James VI and Prince Christian all came. The king who gave the island never saw Uraniborg. (His planned counterpart at Kassel — Wilhelm IV's 1588 voyage to Hven — was likewise cancelled by Frederick's death.)

“Märkligt nog ingick inte stjärnforskarens store mecenat, Fredrik II”

never visitedBnv-vienna

Thoren states Vienna is 'a city that Tycho seems never to have visited'. The Amalienburg clock legend survives only through Rudolf II's posthumous purchase of the instruments, and professional horologists strongly doubt any such Tycho clock exists. The thesaurus movement of Tycho's manuscripts to Vienna (1621) tracks objects after his death, not his travels.

Väsby / Tågalycka (birth of the infant Claus, 2 Jan 1577)

never visitedBnv-vasby-tagalycka-1577
The claim. Tycho was present at the plague refuge (Tågalycka per Christianson, Väsby per Jönsson) for the birth of his son Claus.
Tycho lodged his pregnant wife and daughter away from the plague — at the widow Margrethe Gagge's Tågalycka manor in Christianson's account, at Väsby north of Helsingborg in Jönsson's. The infant Claus was born 2 January 1577 and died six days later; Christianson is explicit that 'Tycho never saw him, but composed a dolorous epitaph for his grave'. Neither source places Tycho at either refuge; the sources' disagreement over the refuge itself is left open. Unpinned: neither manor site is identified.

Brandýs nad Labem (Brandeis)

declinedAnv-brandys-residence
The claim. Tycho resided at Brandýs (Brandeis), the imperial estate Rudolf II offered him in 1599.
Brandeis — the emperor's favourite hunting-lodge — was one of three estates offered in 1599. Tycho inspected it and declined it, taking the smaller hilltop Benátky instead; Thoren suggests he was concerned about depriving the emperor of so grand a property, and it appears in his finances only as a rent source for his salary. His sole attested bodily presence is a datelined letter of 20 August 1599 en route to Benátky — a stop, not a residence.

Benátky (visit by Rudolf II)

disputedBnv-rudolf-benatky
The claim. Rudolf II visited Tycho at Benátky.
An entrance was prepared for the emperor, who reserved an adjoining house — but 'whether Rudolph ever came to Benatky while Tycho was there is not known, and it is not likely', the court sitting out the plague at Pilsen through the winter of 1599–1600. The prepared apartments are evidence of hope, not of a visit; the claim stays in the phantom register until positive evidence appears.

“it is not likely”

Copenhagen (Christian IV's coronation, August 1596)

disputedBnv-coronation-1596
The claim. Tycho attended Christian IV's coronation.
The summons survives — 2 May 1596, commanding the nobility 'at de selv personlig kunne møde hos Kongen' — but only the summons. Friis mentions the coronation's extravagance solely as context for the retrenchments that cost Tycho his fiefs, and Tycho's own letter says merely that he lost Nordfjord 'about Michaelmas straight after the coronation'. Attendance is plausible, but nowhere documented; the chancery rule that invitations do not prove attendance governs.

Becker (ed.), 'Bidrag til Astronomen Tyge Brahes Historie' (Danske Magazin 3. R. IV–V), Friis 1871 p. 227; Danske Magazin 3R Bd 3 pp. 79–80 Coronation as context only; no presence claim.

Gislövgård (Skytts härad, Scania)

disputedCnv-gislovgard
The claim. Tycho was present at Gislövgård when the crown estate changed hands in 1574.
The order of 18 May 1574 commands Tyge Brahe Ottesen to hand over 'Gislom Gaard og Gods' with inventory, letters, registers and land-books to Fru Abbel Breyde. The order documents that he administered the estate, not that he stood on it: the handover's execution and any bodily presence are undocumented. A holding administered on paper; the manor is unpinned, its site unidentified.
Evidence (1)
Kancelliets Brevbøger vedr. Danmarks indre Forhold (Rigsarkivet, ed. Laursen), KancellietsBrevbøger 1571–75 p. 441 Handover order only; presence undocumented.

Hamburg (city proper)

disputedBnv-hamburg-city
The claim. Tycho was bodily present in the city of Hamburg during the Wandsbek year (1597–98).
Wandsbek was chosen precisely for its proximity to Hamburg, and traffic ran inward: the printer Philipp von Ohr came out from Hamburg to set type on Tycho's press at Wandsburg, and the error-ridden Hamburg printing of the Progymnasmata lunar section was supervised by Longomontanus, who stayed behind. No passage consulted states that Tycho entered Hamburg itself. Recorded as absence of evidence, not a denial.
Evidence (2)
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), Christianson 2000 pp. 217, 227; Dreyer 1890 pp. 266, 282 Proximity documented; entry into the city nowhere stated.

Helsingør (Øresund toll chamber)

disputedBnv-helsingor-toll
The claim. Tycho was bodily at Helsingør over the Øresund toll payments that anchored his economy.
The toll chamber paid Tycho repeatedly — fyrpenge for the Kullen light 1581–89, the 400-daler Nordfjord compensation 1586–92, 1050 daler in 1588 — but no chancery entry places him at Helsingør to collect. In the 1594 Pepeler affair the surety at Helsingør was taken by 'Tyge Brahes Tjener paa Tyge Brahes Vegne' — his servant, expressly in his stead. A revenue anchor, not a residence or a documented destination.

disputedBnv-curtius-hven-1594
The claim. Imperial vice-chancellor Jacob Curtius visited Tycho at Hven around 1594 and left a plan of his Prague house.
Gassendi's story of Curtius travelling to Denmark lacks any traceable authority, and Dreyer notes that Curtius is nowhere mentioned in the Meteorological Diary, 'so he can hardly have been at Hveen'. The tale matters because Tycho later died in the Curtius house on Hradčany — a neat narrative arc that the evidence will not carry. Bears on the Hven visitor register, not on Tycho's own itinerary.
Evidence (1)
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 223
“so he can hardly have been at Hveen”

Kronborg Castle

disputedBnv-kronborg
The claim. Tycho was bodily at Kronborg Castle (e.g. at the Garter investiture of Frederick II, 13 August 1582).
The visual tradition — the Frederiksborg-series tapestry showing a nobleman taken to be Tycho behind Frederik II before Kronborg — is a depiction, not evidence. Christianson describes the 13 August 1582 Garter investiture without placing Tycho at it; his documented contact with the English delegation is their sail to Hven on 18 August. Morsing notes only that Kronborg was visible from Uraniborg's west windows. Presence in Helsingør town at other dates rests on other sources; presence at the castle is undocumented here.
Evidence (2)
Tycho Brahes Verden (Nationalmuseet, 2006), Tycho Brahes Verden scan p. 12 (fig. 2); Håkansson ed. 2006 scan p. 51; Morsing 2003 scan pp. 18, 45 Tapestry depiction and king's-speech rhetoric only.
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 116–117 Investiture described without Tycho; delegation visited Hven 18 August 1582.

Kullagården / Kullen lighthouse

disputedBnv-kullen-light
The claim. Tycho was bodily at Kullagården or the Kullen light he was obliged to maintain.
The holding is richly documented — grant 1577, transfer 1580, re-grant 1581 'so long as he stays living on Hven', maintenance orders and rebukes to 1589 — but no chancery entry documents his presence. The 1581 order that Ugerup proceed to Kullagården 'i Forening med Tyge Brahe' survives only as an order, its execution unrecorded; the 1584 tower-relocation commission names others, convened 'after further notice from Tyge Brahe'. His own argument for keeping the farm was fuel for Hven, not residence. The 27 July 1584 tower-relocation commission (Frederiksborg) named Tycho with Gyldenstjerne and Ugerup and a report was submitted, but no source narrates him on the headland; a former C-grade stay on the commission was withdrawn under the presence rule.
Evidence (4)
Kancelliets Brevbøger vedr. Danmarks indre Forhold (Rigsarkivet, ed. Laursen), Kancelliets Brevbøger 1576–79, pp. 230, 249, 765; 1580–83, pp. 123, 295, 378–379, 517, 750; 1584–88, pp. 126, 273, 296, 392; 1588–92, p. 264 Orders survive; execution and presence undocumented.
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 242–250 Fief-administration only; no bodily presence asserted.
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 pp. 148–149
“at de med os elskelige Tyge Brahe til Knudstrup ... skulle begive dem til Kulden ... forfare Lejligheden” the report found the tower ruinous; rebuilding ordered 19 April 1585
Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890), p. 104
“In 1584 the governor of Helsingborg Castle and the chief magistrate of Scania were ordered to proceed to Kullen, together with Tycho, to examine the lighthouse”

Nuremberg (Walther/Regiomontanus balcony)

disputedCnv-nuremberg-walther-balcony
The claim. Tycho visited the Walther/Regiomontanus observing balcony (later Dürer's house) in Nuremberg in 1575.
Purely Christianson's inference from the itinerary: Tycho 'must have seen the high balcony where Walther and Regiomontanus observed the stars'. The Nuremberg pass-through itself is attested and kept as a place-stay; the pilgrimage to the balcony is an editorial embellishment that no source records and that the presence rule cannot admit.
Evidence (1)
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), p. 72
“must have seen the high balcony”

Odense (Latin school)

disputedCnv-odense-school
The claim. Tycho attended the Latin school in Odense.
Pure conjecture in Norlind: that Tycho attended a formal cathedral or Latin school at all is 'mycket ovisst', and Odense enters only as 'perhaps', because Jørgen Brahe was for a time lensmand there (cf. the Næsbyhoved stay). No source documents schooling in Odense; the claim must not generate a childhood stay in the town itself.
Evidence (1)
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), p. 12
“mycket ovisst”

Roskilde (Chapel of the Three Holy Kings prebend)

disputedBnv-roskilde-prebend
The claim. Tycho was bodily in Roskilde on the business of his Helligtrekongers Kapel prebend (1579–97).
No chancery entry places Tycho in Roskilde across the prebend's whole tenure. All chapel business — grace-year, singing duties, the ruinous fabric, the vault-removal permission of 8 November 1594 — was conducted by letter and bailiff; on 1 August 1593 it was the king, not Tycho, who had 'now himself been here in the church and inspected the chapel'. Stays recorded from the biographies keep Roskilde in the gazetteer at grade C; the prebend-visit claim itself fails the presence rule.
Evidence (2)
Kancelliets Brevbøger vedr. Danmarks indre Forhold (Rigsarkivet, ed. Laursen), Kancelliets Brevbøger 1576–79, pp. 662, 664, 682, 784; 1580–83, pp. 200, 520; 1584–88, p. 618; 1588–92, p. 659; 1593–96, pp. 122, 342, 355; 1596–1602, pp. 168, 170 All prebend business by letter; the king inspected the chapel, not Tycho.
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 242–250 Prebend treated as revenue administration.

Roskilde (Frederick II's funeral, June 1588)

disputedCnv-frederik2-funeral-1588
The claim. Tycho attended Frederick II's funeral in Roskilde Cathedral.
Christianson records Rantzau calling at Uraniborg on 27 May 1588 'on his way to the king's funeral in Roskilde', and Tycho's documented lobbying that summer took place on Hven and in Copenhagen (18–23 August). The source is silent on any funeral attendance by Tycho, and no other source supplies it. An attendance that would seem natural for a leading vassal, but which the presence rule cannot pass on silence.
Evidence (1)
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), pp. 129–130 Source silent on Tycho at the funeral; Rantzau went.

Sorø (the claimed Latin-school years, 1559–62)

disputedDnv-soro-schooling
The claim. Schooling at Sorø 1559–62, concurrent with the Copenhagen university years
Asserted only by an earlier compilation of the album leaves, which gives Sorø and Copenhagen identical 1559–62 date-ranges in the same sentence — an internal duplication betraying compression or conflation. No other source places Tycho at Sorø in these years; all ten sources for the period put him at the University of Copenhagen. Recorded in the phantom register rather than as a stay; if a Sorø schooling tradition exists it belongs, undated, to the pre-1559 period.
Evidence (1)
The album-amicorum leaves, in the Graphonomicon, Brahe hand profile §4.1
“Tycho was educated at Sorø (1559–62), Copenhagen (1559–62), Leipzig (1562–65), then Wittenberg, Rostock, Augsburg, and Basel” Same date-range given for Sorø and Copenhagen; internally suspect; graded D on first reading
The sources disagree. Single passing mention, internally inconsistent with the same source's Copenhagen claim, uncorroborated in any other source — removed from the stays to the phantom register.

Veneto academies (Vicenza / Padua, 1575)

disputedBnv-veneto-academies
The claim. Tycho visited Palladio's Accademia Olimpica in Vicenza and the Accademia dei Rinascenti in Padua in 1575.
Christianson offers the academies only as speculative venues: the Venetian discussions 'may have taken place' in them, and 'Tycho did not record the details'. Only Venice itself is asserted for 1575. Padua enters the gazetteer solely at grade D on Jönsson's garden-model conjecture; Vicenza not at all. The academy visits must not be promoted to stays.
Evidence (1)
Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020), pp. 70–71
“may have taken place”

Wartenberg / Brebistorff visits from Benátky (Pentecost 1600)

disputedCnv-benatky-promised-visits-1600
The claim. Tycho carried out the visit promised to Carl von Wartenberg for Pentecost 1600, having declined Gotfred von Brebistorff's invitation.
The letter of 15 May 1600 documents intentions only: a promised visit to Wartenberg (with Ehrenfried von Minckwitz) and a declined invitation from Brebistorff. No follow-up in the sources confirms the Wartenberg journey was ever made. Both are logged so that the promise is not silently upgraded to an executed stay — the declined invitation by definition, the promised visit for want of any evidence of execution.
Evidence (1)
Friis, Breve og Aktstykker (1875), Friis 1875 doc. 40, OCR ll. 6525-6584 Intentions in a letter; no execution documented.

Wittenberg (1568 pass-through, with Castle Neideck)

disputedBnv-wittenberg-1568
The claim. Tycho stayed in Wittenberg (and Leipzig, attending Steen Brahe's dubbing at Castle Neideck) on the 1568 way from Rostock to Basel.
Norlind shows Dreyer's supporting citation points to the wrong edition's foliation and that the Mechanica passage says nothing of 1568 — 'the statement must rest on a misunderstanding'; his summary keeps only 'über Wittenberg (?)'. Christianson likewise hedges: 'possibly through Wittenberg and Leipzig', 'may have been at Castle Neideck'. The 1568 route survives only as a question mark and must not be asserted as stays.
Evidence (2)
Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970), pp. 23–24; Zusammenfassung p. 427

10Editorial method

How the itinerary was made, stated so that it can be checked. The register rests on fourteen readings of the literature — the sources of §12, each read for every statement of where Tycho was and when — and on the documents that fix a presence directly: a dated letter written at a named place, an album leaf signed and dated, an observation entered in the journals with its place, an entry in the meteorological diary kept on Hven. Each source's statements were first recorded as that source's own account, with its page; the accounts were then reconciled, period by period, into the stays, journeys and phantoms printed here. Where the sources agree the stay says so once; where they disagree the record says which reading is followed and why, and the other readings stand beside it under the sources disagree. Nothing was resolved by silence: ninety-two of the hundred and forty stays carry such a note.

The presence rule. A stay asserts that Tycho was bodily at the place. A holding, a grant, a summons, a letter received, an imprint, a presentation copy despatched, an object that travelled — none of these places him, and each kind of claim that has been read as a visit is gathered in the phantom register (§9) with its verdict. A continuous residence is one stay (Hven 1576–1597, Benátky 1599–1600), and the documented absences from it are stays of their own; the visits paid to him at a residence belong to that residence, not to the itinerary. Gassendi's Vita of 1655, the headwater of the whole biographical tradition, is cited as the origin of an anecdote and never as sole authority: a stay resting on Gassendi alone is graded C, and his datings are rejected wherever the journals contradict them.

Grades. A: presence directly and multiply attested. B: attested by one strong source, or a documented station of a route. C: probable, single-source, or regionally imprecise. D: a presence the sources themselves dispute or offer only as conjecture (Kullen, Tågalycka, Malmö, Padua, the unnamed Rantzau castle). A grade is a statement about the evidence for the presence, not about the importance of the place, and no grade is rounded.

Dates and calendars. Danish and Saxon dates are Julian throughout (Denmark kept the old style until 1700); Bohemian dates from 1599 are Gregorian, and the records where the two styles meet carry a calendar note. A stay's precision is that of its best-attested bound; where the other bound is coarser the date says so (a month beside a day). Where an editor's date is followed over another's, the record names both.

Places and coordinates. A place enters the gazetteer (§4) when a stay or a phantom claim needs it. The micro-sites of Hven and Prague — Uraniborg, Stjerneborg, the laboratory, the printing house, the paper mill, the Belvedere, the Curtius house, the Rožmberk palace, the Týn church — are sites (§5) within their place, not places. A coordinate is given only where the location is known; a manor whose site is unidentified, and a region named where no source names a town (Scania, Zealand, Jutland, ‘Denmark’), is left unpinned rather than guessed, and appears in the tables but never on the map.

What the reader can check. Every evidence entry names its source by the short form of §12 and gives the printed page; where a source was read in a digital copy whose printed folio could not be recovered, the copy's page is given as such (§11 lists them). The disagreements the edition has left open, and the readings it has adopted, are all in the records; the desk's own working notes behind them are kept with the data and are not part of the edition.

11Desiderata

What is missing, doubtful or unresolved, named rather than smoothed over. Nothing below is a defect in the sources' sense: each is a place where the evidence stops and the next piece of work begins.

Gazetteer records with no documented stay 9

Each is in the gazetteer for a stated reason. Three — Denmark (family circle), Denmark (residence unspecified) and Denmark (locality unnamed) — were region blobs made to hold imprecisely-located stays that the reconciliation then assigned to named places or to Denmark (unspecified). They are kept because the compilation spec keeps region blobs; whether they should now be retired is an editorial decision, not a data question.

Sites with no link to the object 10

The store carried no external link of any kind before this edition. Four have now been verified and attached (§5). The remaining 10 have none: for the lost and ruined sites there is nothing to link to, but the Belvedere, Benátky castle and the Schwarzenberg palace all stand and are open, and each should carry its institution’s record. Hven (Ven), Uraniborg, The gardens and ramparts of Uraniborg, The alchemical laboratory, The library and the great globe, The printing house (Tycho's press), The Belvedere (Royal Summer Palace), Benátky nad Jizerou, The Curtius (Kurtz) house, The Schwarzenberg (Rožmberk) palace.

People named in the register with no Familia record 126

Of the 502 persons named across the stays, 282 are linked to their record in the Familia pillar. The 126 names without a link have no Familia record — a gap on the Familia side, not a doubt about the person. The most frequent are the household itself: Kirsten Jørgensdatter (22), Jørgen Brahe (16), Inger Oxe (9), Peder Oxe (6), Tycho Tygesen Brahe (6), Mogens Bertelsen Dallin (5), Otte Brahe (4), Knud Brahe (4), Johannes Eriksen (4), Johan Gregor van der Schardt (3), Peter Winstrup (3), Thaddaeus Hagecius (3).

Citations located only by the page of the reference copy 97

Several sources were read in digital copies and first cited by the copy’s page. Where the printed folio could be read from the cited page and agreed with its neighbour, the printed page is now given; where it could not, the citation gives the copy’s page, marked ‘scan p.’, and the source entry in §12 states the offset. By source: Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000) 43; Tycho Brahes Verden (Nationalmuseet, 2006) 18; Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55) 10; Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga (2006) 9; Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (2002) 4; Studnička, Prager Tychoniana (1901) 4; Morsing, Den ukendte Tycho Brahe (2003) 3; Christianson, 'Tycho Brahe's Facts of Life' (1970) 3; Ellefsen, Søsteren og astronomen (2023) 1; Mosley, Bearing the Heavens (2007) 1; The Meteorological Diary 1582–1597 (via the Tychoniana Diarium) 1.

Bibliography

Friis 1871 has no verified open-access scan. The Internet Archive item that answers a search for it is Dreyer’s critical review of Friis, not Friis’s book, and it is deliberately not linked here. Nørlind 1970, Thoren 1990, Christianson 2000 and 2020, Jern 1976 and the Prague Crossroads volume are in copyright and carry no link.

Standing questions 1

Questions the store carries as still open. The other entries in its question log — the modelling of the printed Uraniborg views and of the Prague sites — are resolved and appear in §5.

  1. exact rampart-enclosure dimensions and the full quantified garden plant census from the Hven archaeological reports.

Conflicts left open

The register keeps every disagreement it found rather than resolving it: 92 of the 140 stays carry a “the sources disagree” note. Several are flagged in §10 as needing a return to the primary documents — Thoren’s 14 against 16 September 1566; whether the Augsburg landlords Thenn and Laurentius are one man; whether the Göggingen quadrant was destroyed by the storm of December 1574 or still in use in 1577.

Thirty-eight sources carry the 878 evidence citations in this edition. Each entry gives the full reference, what that source contributes to this reconstruction, how many citations rest on it, and — where an open-access edition has been verified — a link to the text itself. Every citation in the register names its source by the short form used here and links to its entry.
